Offer one when the task is the kind a plugin could take over or make repeatable (deploys, reviews against a team process, or the ticket, data and document workflows a user's org may have packaged as plugins) and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about plugins. Also when they ask for plugin recommendations. First call SearchPlugins with keywords drawn from the task, then pass the relevant results here: pluginId from each result's id, pluginName from its name, description as returned. Set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). Use ListPlugins for plugins they already have.

After the card, continue the task. Example: "ship this to staging" and a deploy plugin that is not enabled → contextLabel "For your deploys".

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a plugin would help, when SearchPlugins returned nothing relevant (then continue the task without mentioning the search), or if you already rendered a plugin or skill suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

contextLabel.description: Short header tying the suggestion to the user request.

tools.name: SuggestSkills
tools.description:
Render a card of standalone skills the user can add — org, shared, or Anthropic skills not yet enabled.

Call this when the task is one a skill could make repeatable — drafting in a house style, reviews against a playbook, a recurring workflow — and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about skills. Also when they ask for recommendations, or when ListSkills returned zero matches. Use ListSkills for skills they already have.

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a skill would help, or if you already rendered a suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

Pass keywords drawn from the task itself, and set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). If the result is empty and the trigger was proactive, continue the task without mentioning that you searched; if the user asked, tell them you found nothing new to add.

keywords.description: Topic keywords from the user's request.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: small — keep workflows under 5 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

tools.name: mcp__1a59c906-04da-521d-bda7-7f71b9f9e01c__batch
tools.description: Create a doc, or apply several operations to one doc atomically.

tools.name: mcp__1a59c906-04da-521d-bda7-7f71b9f9e01c__guide
tools.description: Docs guides: topic.instructions repeats the server instructions. Read it only if your client dropped them. Also topic.<name>, refusal.<code>. After a doc's birth → ["topic.index"].

items.description: topic.<name> (instructions, index, editing, tabs, comments, charts, chart-definition, diagram, uploads, sharing, skill) or refusal.<code>; several per call is fine.

tools.name: mcp__1a59c906-04da-521d-bda7-7f71b9f9e01c__update
tools.description: Edit a tab's contents, rename a doc or tab, or change a stored value.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_directory__change_directory
tools.description: Move this session to a different project directory on the user's computer. Access is granted immediately; the session's working directory (for Bash, relative paths, and project settings) moves there when the current turn ends, so use absolute paths until then. `path` is required — the user sees and approves that exact folder (the user is not asked in bypass permissions mode, or in auto mode when the folder is inside a workspace they trust). Use this when the user's task is about an existing project and the session isn't in it yet; to let the user pick a folder themselves, use request_directory without a path.

path.description: Absolute host path of the folder to move the session to (e.g. ~/code/my-project).

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a proposal you made with start_session (initiation "own_initiative" or "offer") that the user has not started.

Call this when it went stale: the work was done here after all (by you or the user), it turned out unnecessary, or you proposed a better-scoped replacement (propose the new one first, then dismiss the old task_id). A card the user answered has already left, "Do it here" included, so it needs no call.

task_id.description: The task_id the start_session proposal returned.

reason.description: Optional one-line reason the suggestion is no longer needed, e.g. "fixed in this session" or "superseded by task_ab12cd34".

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__hand_off_to_session
tools.description: Move the task you are in the middle of into its own session (a fork of this conversation plus your remaining plan) so you can answer the user now. Use it when a new user message about something else arrives mid-task — not for small corrections or when the user said to keep the work here. In a worktree the fork gets a fresh worktree, normally cut from your branch tip: commit first (uncommitted edits stay here). Bold title line and one sentence right before the call; after it, stop that task here and answer the new message — no recap.

title.description: Under 60 chars; names the task being moved.

remaining_plan.description: What is left to do: steps, files, what done looks like.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

title.description: Short noun-phrase title for the chapter (under 40 chars). Shown in the table of contents.

summary.description: Optional one-line summary of what this chapter covers. Shown on hover in the table of contents.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__read_widget_context
tools.description: Read context from an embedded interactive widget. Widgets are rendered alongside chat from prior tool calls and can be interacted with by the user. Call this when you need to know the current state of a widget.

tool_name.description: The name of the widget tool to get context for

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

scope.description: Required with items: "first_task", "continuation" or "new_task" (see the tool description). Omit on advance / done / start updates.

session.description: When you delegated this step to a session you started: that session's short name (from start_session's result). The app shows its live state on the step.

items.description: The whole plan, in order (1–12 steps); replaces the previous list.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available, or one your own work this turn made available; others are refused, and one that later stops being available is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and other answers), so do not guess. Offer commit, create_pr or verify only once the work the user asked for is done, not every turn. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Not now": a button, not a sentence. A click sends it to you as the user's answer. Never a go-ahead to commit: that is the commit app action. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments. Never repeat an offer the user passed over, as an app action, a reply or a question in your closing message, unless what it acts on has changed since or they bring it up.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, form_input, read_page). browser_batch cannot be nested. A tabs_create's new tabId is only returned when the batch ends — load that tab in a later call.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","ref":"ref_12"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"screenshot"}}]

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__find
tools.description: Search the current page in the Browser pane for elements whose accessibility-tree line (role / name / text) contains `query`, case-insensitively. Returns up to 20 `ref_N` matches usable with `computer`/`form_input`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

query.description: Text to look for in an element's role, name or text (case-insensitive substring, e.g. "Sign in", "search", "Add to cart").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__form_input
tools.description: Set the value of a form element identified by `ref` (from read_page/find). Handles input/textarea/select/checkbox/contenteditable.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

ref.description: Element reference ID from the read_page tool (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2")

value.description: The value to set. For checkboxes use boolean, for selects use option value or text, for other inputs use appropriate string/number

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this form fill does on the page and to what, for example 'Sets the delivery date to 29 September'. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__get_page_text
tools.description: Extract the visible text of the Browser pane's page (article/main content first, falls back to body innerText).

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__javascript_tool
tools.description: Execute JavaScript in the Browser pane's page for DEBUGGING and INSPECTION only. Do NOT use this to implement UI changes — edit source code instead.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description: Action to perform (only `javascript_exec` is supported).

text.description: The JavaScript code to execute. Evaluated in the page context with REPL semantics: top-level `await` works, and the result of the last expression is returned automatically — write the expression you want (e.g. `window.myData.value`, or `await fetch(url).then(r=>r.json())`) rather than `return ...`. Return values are serialized as JSON.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__navigate
tools.description: Navigate the Browser pane to a URL, or go "back"/"forward" in history. If the Browser pane isn't open yet, this opens it at the URL (no dev server needed).

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

url.description: The URL to navigate to. Can be provided with or without protocol (defaults to https://). Use "forward" to go forward in history or "back" to go back in history.

force.description: If the page shows a "Leave site?" dialog because of unsaved changes, discard those changes and navigate anyway. Defaults to false.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__preview_list
tools.description: List servers started with preview_start. Returns serverIds for use with other preview_* tools.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__preview_logs
tools.description: Get server stdout/stderr output. Use to check for build errors, verify server behavior, or read debug output. Use 'level' to filter to errors only, or 'search' to filter for specific text. Use after preview_start.

level.description: Filter by level: 'all' (default) shows all output, 'error' shows only lines containing error/exception/failed/fatal

search.description: Filter to lines containing this text (e.g., '[DEBUG]', 'POST /api')

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__preview_start

name.description: Server name from .claude/launch.json.

url.description: URL to open in the Browser pane without a dev server (instead of starting one by `name`).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__preview_stop
tools.description: Stop a server started with preview_start.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__read_console_messages
tools.description: Get console output (log, info, warn, error, debug) from the Browser pane.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

limit.description: Max entries to return (default: 50, max: 200).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__read_network_requests
tools.description: List network requests, or fetch a specific response body by `requestId`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

urlPattern.description: Substring filter on the request URL as listed (auth values show as REDACTED).

requestId.description: If provided, returns the response body for this request instead of listing.

limit.description: Max entries to return when listing (default: 50).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__read_page
tools.description: Read the current page in the Browser pane as a YAML-style accessibility tree. Each interactive element is tagged `[ref_N]` for use with `computer`/`form_input`/`find`. Prefer this over screenshot for verifying text and structure. Output is limited to 50000 characters by default; if it exceeds the limit it is truncated with a note — pass a larger max_chars, or use ref_id/depth to focus.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

filter.description: 'interactive' returns only clickable/typable elements; 'all' (default) returns the full tree.

ref_id.description: Restrict the tree to descendants of this `ref_N` (from a previous read_page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'press_key' presses a hardware key 'count' times: return, delete (backspace), an arrow, select_all, undo or redo (a key also hides the on-screen keyboard); 'set_appearance' switches the device to light or dark mode; 'appearance' says which it is in; 'set_keyboard' shows or hides the on-screen keyboard (it appears only while a text field has focus, and 'press_key' and 'text' hide it again); 'rotate' turns the device a quarter turn left or right ('direction'); take a 'screenshot' after it and tap in that screenshot's frame, however it comes back; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). points2.description: For 'touch2_path': two-finger path samples in device points. Each sample carries both contacts (x1/y1, x2/y2); first is touch-down, last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000 ms; the first sample's is skipped, so send 0 or omit it; at most 30 seconds in all).

# Lesson 7 — A LangGraph agent with graph tools

Lesson 6 described giving an agent tools over the graph. Here we build it with
[LangGraph](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/) and any **OpenAI-compatible** chat endpoint.

## Setup

In `.env` (see [.env.example](../.env.example)):

```bash
LLM_BASE_URL=https://api.deepinfra.com/v1   # or OpenAI, OpenRouter, Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM...
LLM_MODEL=google/gemma-4-31B-it              # must support tool calling
LLM_API_KEY=...
```

`config.chat_model()` builds a LangChain `ChatOpenAI` pointed at that endpoint, so swapping
providers is an `.env` change, not a code change. Recorded outputs used DeepInfra with
`google/gemma-4-31B-it`.

## LangGraph in one picture

A LangGraph app is a **state machine**: a typed state, **nodes** (functions that return state
updates) and **edges** (which node runs next, possibly chosen by a function).

```
START ──► agent ──(tool calls?)──► tools ──┐
            ▲                              │
            └──────────────────────────────┘
          (no tool calls) ──► END
```

```python
g = StateGraph(MessagesState)                    # state = the message list
g.add_node("agent", agent)                       # LLM with tools bound
g.add_node("tools", ToolNode(TOOLS))             # runs whatever tools the LLM asked for
g.add_edge(START, "agent")
g.add_conditional_edges("agent", tools_condition)  # -> "tools" if tool calls, else END
g.add_edge("tools", "agent")
app = g.compile(checkpointer=InMemorySaver())    # remembers messages per thread_id
```

The **checkpointer** is LangGraph's short-term memory: every turn on the same `thread_id`
sees the earlier messages. (Lessons 8–10 add *long-term* memory in Neo4j.)

## The tools — [`team_agent.py`](../team_agent.py)

| Tool | Kind | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `find_experts(skill)` | fixed, parameterized | people with a skill, strongest first, plus their active projects |
| `person_profile(name)` | fixed | role, bio, skills, projects, manager, contacts |
| `staffing_gaps()` | fixed | required skills only 0–1 people have (Lesson 1 query 9) |
| `semantic_search(text)` | vector | Lesson 5's `embedded_vec` index |
| `run_cypher(query)` | free-form | read-only Cypher, schema in the docstring, 25-row cap |

Every tool runs inside `session.execute_read(...)`, so Neo4j itself rejects writes:

```python
>>> run_cypher.invoke({"query": "CREATE (:Person {name:'Hacker'})"})
Query failed: {neo4j_code: Neo.ClientError.Statement.AccessMode}
{message: Writing in read access mode not allowed. Attempted write to neo4j} ...
```

The tool's **docstring is the tool description** the LLM sees, which is why `run_cypher`
carries the schema.

## Run it

```bash
.venv/bin/python team_agent.py                                   # interactive
.venv/bin/python team_agent.py "Who could back up Eve if she's out for a month?"
```

## Output ([full log](outputs/07-team-agent.txt))

```
You: Who could back up Eve if she's out for a month?
  → person_profile({"name": "Eve"})
  ← person_profile: {"name": "Eve", "role": "Data Scientist", ... "skills": ["Python (le…
  → find_experts({"skill": "ML"})
  → find_experts({"skill": "Python"})
  ← find_experts: [{"person": "Eve", "level": 5, "active_projects": ["Search Revamp"]}]
  ← find_experts: [{"person": "Alice", "level": 5, ...}, {"person": "Eve", "level": 4, ...}, {"person": "Gia", …
  → run_cypher({"query": "MATCH (p:Person)-[:HAS_SKILL]->(s:Skill) WHERE s.name IN ['ML', 'Machine Learning', 'Data Science'] RETURN p.name, s.name"})
  ← run_cypher: [{"p.name": "Eve", "s.name": "ML"}]

Agent: ... Alice is the strongest candidate for backup. She is also working on the Search
Revamp project and possesses a higher proficiency in Python (level 5) than Eve. Gia also has
Python skills (level 3) ... However, Eve appears to be the only person with the ML skill ...
making her a single point of failure for the machine learning aspects of the Search Revamp project.
```

```
You: Which active projects are at risk because only one person has a required skill, and who could we train?
  → staffing_gaps({})
  ← staffing_gaps: [{"project": "Search Revamp", "skill": "ML", "who": ["Eve"]}, {"project": "Mobile App", "skill": "UX", "who": ["Bob"]}]
  → find_experts({"skill": "ML"})
  → find_experts({"skill": "UX"})
  ...
Agent: ... For ML (Search Revamp): Alice ... proficient in Python, which is commonly used for ML.
For UX (Mobile App): Cara ... already building React Native components and a shared design system.
```

```
You: How many people does Dev manage, and what are their roles?
  → run_cypher({"query": "MATCH (m:Person {name: 'Dev'})-[:MANAGES]->(e:Person)
                OPTIONAL MATCH (e)-[:HAS_ROLE]->(r:Role) RETURN e.name AS employee, r.name AS role"})
  ← run_cypher: [{"employee": "Finn", "role": "Senior Engineer"}, {"employee": "Cara", "role": "Engineer"}, {"employee": "Alice", "role": "Engineer"}]

Agent: Dev manages 3 people: Finn (Senior Engineer), Cara (Engineer), Alice (Engineer)
```

What to notice:
- The model **calls tools in parallel** (two `find_experts` at once) — `ToolNode` runs them together.
- It **chains**: profile → experts → a custom Cypher check.
- For a question no fixed tool covers, it **wrote correct Cypher**, including the `:Role` nodes
  from Lesson 3, using only the schema in the docstring.

## Takeaways

- Start with **fixed, parameterized tools**; add free-form Cypher behind a read-only transaction.
- Put the **schema in the tool description** so the model can write queries.
- LangGraph's checkpointer gives **short-term** memory per thread; long-term memory needs a store.

# Lesson 8 — Designing memory for an AI assistant / companion

The goal: an assistant that knows the person's **life story** — people, places, history, plans,
preferences, how they're feeling — across many conversations, and updates that knowledge when
life changes. This lesson is the design; Lessons 9–10 build it.

## What a companion needs to remember

| Kind | Example | Lifetime | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| **fact** | "Alex's sister Maya is a nurse in Denver" | until it changes | biography |
| **preference** | "Alex likes quiet mornings and hates phone calls" | until it changes | personalization |
| **event** | "Alex's presentation was praised on 2026-11-12" | permanent, dated | life timeline |
| **plan** | "Maya visits for Thanksgiving on 2026-11-26" | open → done | proactive follow-ups |
| **feeling** | "Alex was nervous about the presentation" | fades within days | empathy, tone |
| **boundary** | "Don't bring up Alex's ex, Jordan" | until revoked | trust and safety |

Plus two things that aren't single memories:
- **The life graph**: who and what is in their life and how they relate (sister, pet, employer).
- **Episodes**: each conversation, with a summary and mood, linked in order — the "diary".

## Why graph + vectors (not just a vector store)

| Need | Vectors alone | Graph + vectors |
|---|---|---|
| "How's my sister?" → find Maya | ✅ fuzzy match | ✅ alias "my sister" → Maya, then hop |
| Everything about Maya | ❌ only text that *looks* similar | ✅ `(m)-[:ABOUT]->(Maya)` |
| "I moved to Seattle" replaces "lives in Portland" | ❌ both stay, contradicting | ✅ `SUPERSEDES` + `invalidated_at` |
| What was true in March? | ❌ | ✅ bi-temporal properties |
| Life timeline, open plans | ❌ | ✅ ordered by `occurred_on` / `due_on` |
| Never surface the ex | ❌ | ✅ exclude entities a boundary is `ABOUT` |
| Where did this memory come from? | ❌ | ✅ `(m)-[:FROM]->(Episode)` |

## The schema — [`companion/schema.py`](../companion/schema.py)

```
(:User:Entity {id, name, kind:'self'})
      │ RELATED {type: sister|pet|works_at|lives_in…, since}
      ▼
(:Entity {id, user, name, kind, aliases[], summary, embedding})   person|pet|place|organization|activity|thing
      ▲ ABOUT
      │
(:Memory {id, user, text, kind, importance 1-10, embedding,
          occurred_on, due_on, status,                 ← domain time: when it happened / is due
          created_at, invalidated_at,                  ← system time: when we learned / un-learned it
          last_accessed, access_count})                ← usage, for recency and reinforcement
      │ SUPERSEDES ──► (:Memory)  older version
      │ FROM ──────► (:Episode {id, user, started_at, ended_at, summary, mood, embedding})
                                  │ NEXT ──► (:Episode)
                                  │ HAS_TURN ──► (:Turn {idx, role, text, at})
```

Design choices, and where they come from in earlier lessons:

- **Memory is a node, not a relationship** (Lesson 3.2): a memory connects to *several*
  entities, has its own properties, and other things point at it (`SUPERSEDES`, `FROM`).
- **Entities are shared nodes** (Lesson 3.1): "who else is in Alex's life?" is a hop, and
  aliases ("my sister", "Mom") resolve to one node.
- **`MERGE` everything that has identity** (Lesson 2): the same Maya across 100 conversations.
- **Two time axes**: `occurred_on`/`due_on` say when something is true in the person's life;
  `created_at`/`invalidated_at` say when the system learned or retired it. Old facts are
  **retired, not deleted**, so history survives ("Alex used to live in Portland").
- **`user` property on every node** scopes all queries and vector searches to one person.
- **Three vector indexes** (Lesson 5): `memory_vec`, `entity_vec`, `episode_vec` (384-dim,
  local `bge-small` model, no API key).

## Design principles for companion memory

1. **Write standalone memories.** "Alex's sister Maya is a nurse", never "she's a nurse" — each
   memory must make sense alone, years later. Same for dates: absolute, never "next Thursday".
2. **Update, don't accumulate.** New information supersedes old; duplicates reinforce.
3. **Importance and recency both matter.** Retrieval ranks by similarity, importance and how
   recently a memory was used; feelings decay in ~a week, facts over months.
4. **Proactivity comes from plans.** Open plans near their due date are always in context, so
   the companion asks "how did it go?" instead of waiting to be told.
5. **Boundaries are hard filters**, applied in the query (not just the prompt), and the
   boundary itself is always in context.
6. **The user owns their memory**: inspect (`/memories`, `/timeline`, `/people`), see history
   (`/history`), and **hard-delete** (`/forget`) — privacy beats provenance for explicit requests.
7. **Never invent.** The extractor records only what the user said or confirmed; the companion
   is told to ask rather than guess.

## Create the schema

```bash
.venv/bin/python -c "from neo4j import GraphDatabase; import config; from companion.schema import ensure_schema; \
d = GraphDatabase.driver(config.NEO4J_URI, auth=config.NEO4J_AUTH); ensure_schema(d); print('ok')"
```

(`MemoryStore(...)` also runs it automatically.)

```cypher
SHOW INDEXES YIELD name, type WHERE name IN ['memory_vec','entity_vec','episode_vec','memory_user_kind']
```

# Lesson 9 — The write path: from conversation to graph

After every exchange, the companion turns what was said into structured memory:

```
exchange ──► extract (LLM, structured output) ──► resolve entities ──► link relations
         ──► retire / complete old memories ──► dedupe ──► create memories (+ SUPERSEDES)
```

Code: [`companion/extract.py`](../companion/extract.py) (LLM),
[`companion/models.py`](../companion/models.py) (the output schema),
[`companion/store.py`](../companion/store.py) `MemoryStore.apply()`.

## 1. Extraction with structured output

The extractor gets the latest user message and reply, **today's date** (to resolve "next
Thursday"), the **known entities**, and the **existing memories it may update, with their ids**
(found by vector search on the user's message, plus every open plan). It returns an `Extraction`:

```python
class Extraction(BaseModel):
    entities: list[EntityOut]        # name, kind, aliases, summary
    relations: list[RelationOut]     # source ('user' or name), target, type, since
    memories: list[MemoryOut]        # text, kind, about, importance, occurred_on, due_on, supersedes
    invalidate: list[str]            # ids no longer true, no replacement
    completed_plans: list[str]       # ids of plans that happened / were cancelled
```

`llm.with_structured_output(Extraction, method="function_calling")` works on any endpoint
with tool calling; the code falls back to "reply with JSON matching this schema" for endpoints
without it. Extraction errors are caught so **memory problems never break the conversation**.

Key prompt rules (see `EXTRACT_SYSTEM`): one standalone third-person sentence per memory,
absolute dates, only what the user said, supersede instead of duplicating, list the protected
person in a boundary's `about`.

## 2. Entity resolution

`resolve_entity(name, kind, aliases, summary)`:

1. "user", "me" or the user's name → the `:User` node
2. exact match on name **or any alias** (case-insensitive)
3. vector match on `entity_vec`, same kind, score ≥ 0.93 ("Mom" ≈ "my mother")
4. otherwise create it

Then aliases are merged (`apoc.coll.toSet`) and the embedding refreshed. Names used in
memories/relations are looked up but **never auto-created**, which avoids junk nodes.

## 3. Dedupe, supersede, retire

| Situation | What happens |
|---|---|
| New memory ≥ 0.975 similar to a current one | **reinforce** the old one (`access_count`, `last_confirmed`, max importance) |
| Extractor lists `supersedes: [id]` | new memory created, old gets `invalidated_at`, `(new)-[:SUPERSEDES]->(old)` |
| `invalidate: [id]` | old gets `invalidated_at`, no replacement |
| `completed_plans: [id]` | plan `status = 'done'` (it stays on the timeline) |

### Tested without an LLM (hand-written extractions)

```
['linked user -sister-> Maya', 'linked Maya -lives_in-> Denver', 'linked user -pet-> Biscuit',
 '+ [fact] Testy lives in Portland', "+ [fact] Testy's sister Maya is a nurse in Denver",
 '+ [plan] Testy has a job interview at Acme on 2026-11-07', '+ [boundary] Testy prefers not to talk about their ex']

# second batch: the same Portland fact again, plus a move that supersedes it
['reinforced m_c4a8a5', '+ [fact] Testy moved to Seattle in October 2026  (replaces m_c4a8a5)']

history: [('Testy moved to Seattle in October 2026', retired=False), ('Testy lives in Portland', retired=True)]
```

## 4. Real extraction log (from the [demo](outputs/10-companion-demo.txt))

The `✎` lines are what `remember` wrote after each reply:

```
Alex: Hi! I'm Alex. I moved to Portland last month for a new job as a UX researcher at Lumen Health.
   ✎ linked user -lives_in-> Portland
   ✎ linked user -works_at-> Lumen Health
   ✎ + [fact] Alex moved to Portland in October 2026.
   ✎ + [fact] Alex works as a UX researcher at Lumen Health.

Alex: Honestly I'm a bit nervous — I'm giving my first big presentation to leadership next Thursday.
   ✎ + [plan] Alex is giving their first big presentation to leadership on 2026-11-12.

— a week later —
Alex: It went really well actually! My VP said it was the clearest research readout she's seen.
   ✎ plan done m_d8e5d4
   ✎ + [event] Alex received high praise from their VP for a research readout presentation on 2026-11-12 ...

Alex: Also, small update: I switched teams, I'm on the Research Ops team now instead of the patient app team.
   ✎ + [fact] Alex works on the Research Ops team at Lumen Health.  (replaces m_0c596b)
```

"Last month" became "October 2026" and "next Thursday" became `2026-11-12`, because the extractor
knows today's date and the prompt forbids relative dates.

> **Before that rule was added**, the first run stored "…presentation to leadership next
> Thursday" — true for one week, then wrong. Prompt rules are part of the data model.

## Inspect it in the Browser

```cypher
// The life graph
MATCH path = (:User {id:'user:alex (demo)'})-[:RELATED]->() RETURN path
```
```cypher
// Memories with what they're about, their versions and their source episode
MATCH p = (m:Memory {user:'user:alex (demo)'})-[:ABOUT|SUPERSEDES|FROM]->() RETURN p
```
```
ABOUT 12, FROM 10, SUPERSEDES 1   (2 episodes, 4 related entities + the user, 10 memories)
```
```cypher
// Episodes in order, with turn counts
MATCH (ep:Episode {user:'user:alex (demo)'})
RETURN ep.started_at, COUNT { (ep)-[:HAS_TURN]->() } AS turns, EXISTS { (ep)-[:NEXT]->() } AS has_next
ORDER BY ep.started_at
```
```
2026-11-05T12:00Z, 8, TRUE
2026-11-13T12:00Z, 6, FALSE
```

# Lesson 10 — Recall, the LangGraph companion, and the terminal chat

## The read path: hybrid recall — `MemoryStore.recall()`

Every user message triggers one recall that combines five sources:

| Source | How | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Core profile** | all boundaries + top 8 facts/preferences (importance ≥ 6) | always know who they are and what to avoid |
| **Semantic** | `memory_vec` top 50 → re-ranked, top 8 | what's relevant to *this* message |
| **Entity hop** | names/aliases in the message + `entity_vec`, then `(m)-[:ABOUT]->(e)` | "how's my sister?" pulls everything about Maya |
| **Follow-ups** | open plans due within ±14 days | proactive "how did it go?" |
| **Recent episodes** | last 3 summaries + mood | continuity between sessions |

Semantic re-ranking (the "generative agents" recipe):

```cypher
0.6 * similarity + 0.25 * importance / 10
  + 0.15 * exp(-days_since_last_used / CASE m.kind WHEN 'feeling' THEN 7.0 ELSE 90.0 END)
```

Filters applied **in Cypher**, not left to the prompt:
- retired memories (`invalidated_at`) and finished plans (`status = 'done'`) are skipped
- entities a boundary is `ABOUT` never appear in the people list or the entity hop

Recalled memories get `last_accessed`/`access_count` updated, so memories the companion uses
stay fresh.

### Boundary filter test

```
memories: boundary "does not want to discuss their ex, Jordan" (about Jordan) + an event about Jordan
recall("I ran into Jordan today"):
  people:     ['Maya']                       ← Jordan excluded
  entity hop: []                             ← even though the message names Jordan
  core:       ['Boundary Test does not want to discuss their ex, Jordan']   ← rule stays visible
```

## The companion graph — [`companion/graph.py`](../companion/graph.py)

```
START ──► recall ──► respond ──► remember ──► END
```

| Node | Does | Memory layer |
|---|---|---|
| `recall` | `store.recall(last message)` → formatted memory block | long-term (Neo4j) |
| `respond` | persona + memory block + last 16 messages → LLM | short-term (checkpointer) |
| `remember` | log turns to the Episode, extract, `store.apply()` | writes long-term |

State extends `MessagesState` with `memory_context` and `memory_log`. The episode id is the
LangGraph `thread_id`; a `today` value can be passed in `config["configurable"]` (the demo uses
it to simulate a week passing).

Two extras make it feel like a companion rather than a chatbot:
- **`greeting()`** opens each session from memory (follow up on due plans, or pick up from last
  time), and `seed_thread()` puts it into the thread with `app.update_state(..., as_node="respond")`.
- **Episode summaries** at `/new` or `/quit` become the diary used for continuity.

## Terminal chat

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m companion                  # uses COMPANION_USER / COMPANION_NAME from .env
.venv/bin/python -m companion --user Sam --debug   # --debug prints the memory block each turn
```

| Command | |
|---|---|
| `/memories [kind]` | current memories (ids, kind, importance, status) |
| `/all` | including retired ones |
| `/people` | the life graph |
| `/timeline` | events and plans by date |
| `/history <id>` | a memory and the versions it replaced |
| `/forget <id>` | hard-delete a memory |
| `/recall <text>` | show exactly what would be recalled for a message |
| `/debug` | toggle the memory block display |
| `/new` | save this episode (summary + mood) and start a new one |
| `/quit` | save and exit |

Smoke test (piped input):

```
Sage: Hi CLI Test, I'm Sage. I'd love to get to know you — how's your day going?
CLI Test: I just started learning the cello, my teacher is named Ines.
Sage: That's exciting! The cello has such a beautiful, rich sound. How are you finding it so far? ...
  ✎ linked user -student_of-> Ines
  ✎ + [fact] CLI Test started learning the cello on 2026-11-05.
CLI Test: /memories
  m_584be0  [fact] CLI Test started learning the cello on 2026-11-05.  ★5
CLI Test: /people
  Ines — student_of (person)
CLI Test: /quit
  ✎ episode saved: On 2026-11-05, CLI Test shared that they have begun learning the cello ... (mood: Excited and optimistic)
```

## The two-session demo — [`companion/demo.py`](../companion/demo.py)

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m companion.demo
```

It uses a separate user, `Alex (demo)`, and wipes it first. Full output:
[outputs/10-companion-demo.txt](outputs/10-companion-demo.txt). Highlights:

Maya, beagle Biscuit, nervous about a presentation "next Thursday", asks not to bring up their ex.

**Session 2 (2026-11-13)** — the companion opens with:

```

```

It remembered the plan, knew its date was 2026-11-12, and knew today is the 13th. Then:

```

Sage: ... Since you're bringing Biscuit along, you could try Forest Park ...
```

It connected Maya, Portland and the dog without being told the dog's name in this session.

**Final state:**

```

  Lumen Health — works_at (organization)
  Maya — sister (person)
  Biscuit — pet (pet)
  Portland — lives_in (place)

/timeline
  2026-11-12  [event] Alex received high praise from their VP for a research readout presentation on 2026-11-12 ...
  2026-11-12  [plan] Alex is giving their first big presentation to leadership on 2026-11-12. [done]
  2026-11-26  [plan] Alex's sister Maya is visiting Alex in Portland for Thanksgiving on 2026-11-26. [open]

  now: Alex works on the Research Ops team at Lumen Health.

**What the LLM sees** for `"what should we do when my sister visits?"`:

The first run (before these fixes) showed five problems. Each one is now handled in code or prompt:

| Problem seen | Fix |
|---|---|

| Core profile only had the boundary (threshold ★8) | core = boundaries + top 8 facts/preferences ★6+ |
| Both episodes dated with the real clock | `start_episode(on=...)` for simulated dates |
| Finished plan still in "Relevant memories" | skip `status = 'done'` in recall |
| The ex appeared in the people list | exclude entities a boundary is `ABOUT` |

## Where to go next

- **Run extraction in the background** (a queue or `asyncio` task) so replies never wait on it.
- **Consolidation job**: periodically merge related memories, update entity summaries, and
  decay or archive low-importance, never-used memories.
- **Graph embeddings** (`gds.fastRP`) on the life graph to find related people and themes.
- **Multi-user / multi-agent**: the `user` property already scopes everything; add an `agent`
  property to give several personas their own view of the same person.
- **Evaluation**: script conversations with known facts, then check recall precision and
  whether boundaries ever leak.

1	# Lesson 10 — Recall, the LangGraph companion, and the terminal chat
2	
3	## The read path: hybrid recall — `MemoryStore.recall()`
4	
5	Every user message triggers one recall that combines five sources:
6	
7	| Source | How | Why |
8	|---|---|---|
9	| **Core profile** | all boundaries + top 8 facts/preferences (importance ≥ 6) | always know who they are and what to avoid |
10	| **Semantic** | `memory_vec` top 50 → re-ranked, top 8 | what's relevant to *this* message |
11	| **Entity hop** | names/aliases in the message + `entity_vec`, then `(m)-[:ABOUT]->(e)` | "how's my sister?" pulls everything about Maya |
12	| **Follow-ups** | open plans due within ±14 days | proactive "how did it go?" |
13	| **Recent episodes** | last 3 summaries + mood | continuity between sessions |
14	
15	Semantic re-ranking (the "generative agents" recipe):
16	
17	```cypher
18	0.6 * similarity + 0.25 * importance / 10
19	  + 0.15 * exp(-days_since_last_used / CASE m.kind WHEN 'feeling' THEN 7.0 ELSE 90.0 END)
20	```
21	
22	Filters applied **in Cypher**, not left to the prompt:
23	- retired memories (`invalidated_at`) and finished plans (`status = 'done'`) are skipped
24	- entities a boundary is `ABOUT` never appear in the people list or the entity hop
25	
26	Recalled memories get `last_accessed`/`access_count` updated, so memories the companion uses
27	stay fresh.

49	| `remember` | log turns to the Episode, extract, `store.apply()` | writes long-term |
50	
51	State extends `MessagesState` with `memory_context` and `memory_log`. The episode id is the
52	LangGraph `thread_id`; a `today` value can be passed in `config["configurable"]` (the demo uses

71	| `/people` | the life graph |
72	| `/timeline` | events and plans by date |
73	| `/history <id>` | a memory and the versions it replaced |
74	| `/forget <id>` | hard-delete a memory |
75	| `/recall <text>` | show exactly what would be recalled for a message |
76	| `/debug` | toggle the memory block display |
77	| `/new` | save this episode (summary + mood) and start a new one |

1	# Lesson 9 — The write path: from conversation to graph
2	
3	After every exchange, the companion turns what was said into structured memory:
4	
5	```
6	exchange ──► extract (LLM, structured output) ──► resolve entities ──► link relations
7	         ──► retire / complete old memories ──► dedupe ──► create memories (+ SUPERSEDES)
8	```
9	
10	Code: [`companion/extract.py`](../companion/extract.py) (LLM),
11	[`companion/models.py`](../companion/models.py) (the output schema),
12	[`companion/store.py`](../companion/store.py) `MemoryStore.apply()`.
13	
14	## 1. Extraction with structured output
15	
16	The extractor gets the latest user message and reply, **today's date** (to resolve "next
17	Thursday"), the **known entities**, and the **existing memories it may update, with their ids**
18	(found by vector search on the user's message, plus every open plan). It returns an `Extraction`:
19	
20	```python
21	class Extraction(BaseModel):
22	    entities: list[EntityOut]        # name, kind, aliases, summary
23	    relations: list[RelationOut]     # source ('user' or name), target, type, since
24	    memories: list[MemoryOut]        # text, kind, about, importance, occurred_on, due_on, supersedes
25	    invalidate: list[str]            # ids no longer true, no replacement
26	    completed_plans: list[str]       # ids of plans that happened / were cancelled
27	```
28	
29	`llm.with_structured_output(Extraction, method="function_calling")` works on any endpoint
30	with tool calling; the code falls back to "reply with JSON matching this schema" for endpoints
31	without it. Extraction errors are caught so **memory problems never break the conversation**.
32	
33	Key prompt rules (see `EXTRACT_SYSTEM`): one standalone third-person sentence per memory,
34	absolute dates, only what the user said, supersede instead of duplicating, list the protected
35	person in a boundary's `about`.
36	
37	## 2. Entity resolution
38	
39	`resolve_entity(name, kind, aliases, summary)`:
40	
41	1. "user", "me" or the user's name → the `:User` node
42	2. exact match on name **or any alias** (case-insensitive)
43	3. vector match on `entity_vec`, same kind, score ≥ 0.93 ("Mom" ≈ "my mother")
44	4. otherwise create it
45	
46	Then aliases are merged (`apoc.coll.toSet`) and the embedding refreshed. Names used in
47	memories/relations are looked up but **never auto-created**, which avoids junk nodes.
48	
49	## 3. Dedupe, supersede, retire
50	
51	| Situation | What happens |
52	|---|---|
53	| New memory ≥ 0.975 similar to a current one | **reinforce** the old one (`access_count`, `last_confirmed`, max importance) |
54	| Extractor lists `supersedes: [id]` | new memory created, old gets `invalidated_at`, `(new)-[:SUPERSEDES]->(old)` |
55	| `invalidate: [id]` | old gets `invalidated_at`, no replacement |
56	| `completed_plans: [id]` | plan `status = 'done'` (it stays on the timeline) |
57	
58	### Tested without an LLM (hand-written extractions)
59	
60	```
61	['linked user -sister-> Maya', 'linked Maya -lives_in-> Denver', 'linked user -pet-> Biscuit',
62	 '+ [fact] Testy lives in Portland', "+ [fact] Testy's sister Maya is a nurse in Denver",
63	 '+ [plan] Testy has a job interview at Acme on 2026-11-07', '+ [boundary] Testy prefers not to talk about their ex']
64	
65	# second batch: the same Portland fact again, plus a move that supersedes it
66	['reinforced m_c4a8a5', '+ [fact] Testy moved to Seattle in October 2026  (replaces m_c4a8a5)']
67	
68	history: [('Testy moved to Seattle in October 2026', retired=False), ('Testy lives in Portland', retired=True)]
69	```
70	
71	## 4. Real extraction log (from the [demo](outputs/10-companion-demo.txt))
72	
73	The `✎` lines are what `remember` wrote after each reply:
74	
75	```
76	Alex: Hi! I'm Alex. I moved to Portland last month for a new job as a UX researcher at Lumen Health.
77	   ✎ linked user -lives_in-> Portland
78	   ✎ linked user -works_at-> Lumen Health
79	   ✎ + [fact] Alex moved to Portland in October 2026.
80	   ✎ + [fact] Alex works as a UX researcher at Lumen Health.
81	
82	Alex: Honestly I'm a bit nervous — I'm giving my first big presentation to leadership next Thursday.
83	   ✎ + [plan] Alex is giving their first big presentation to leadership on 2026-11-12.
84	
85	— a week later —
86	Alex: It went really well actually! My VP said it was the clearest research readout she's seen.
87	   ✎ plan done m_d8e5d4
88	   ✎ + [event] Alex received high praise from their VP for a research readout presentation on 2026-11-12 ...
89	
90	Alex: Also, small update: I switched teams, I'm on the Research Ops team now instead of the patient app team.
91	   ✎ + [fact] Alex works on the Research Ops team at Lumen Health.  (replaces m_0c596b)
92	```
93	
94	"Last month" became "October 2026" and "next Thursday" became `2026-11-12`, because the extractor
95	knows today's date and the prompt forbids relative dates.
96	
97	> **Before that rule was added**, the first run stored "…presentation to leadership next
98	> Thursday" — true for one week, then wrong. Prompt rules are part of the data model.
99	
100	## Inspect it in the Browser
101	
102	```cypher
103	// The life graph
104	MATCH path = (:User {id:'user:alex (demo)'})-[:RELATED]->() RETURN path
105	```
106	```cypher
107	// Memories with what they're about, their versions and their source episode
108	MATCH p = (m:Memory {user:'user:alex (demo)'})-[:ABOUT|SUPERSEDES|FROM]->() RETURN p
109	```
110	```
111	ABOUT 12, FROM 10, SUPERSEDES 1   (2 episodes, 4 related entities + the user, 10 memories)
112	```
113	```cypher
114	// Episodes in order, with turn counts
115	MATCH (ep:Episode {user:'user:alex (demo)'})
116	RETURN ep.started_at, COUNT { (ep)-[:HAS_TURN]->() } AS turns, EXISTS { (ep)-[:NEXT]->() } AS has_next
117	ORDER BY ep.started_at
118	```
119	```
120	2026-11-05T12:00Z, 8, TRUE
121	2026-11-13T12:00Z, 6, FALSE
122	```

1	# Lesson 8 — Designing memory for an AI assistant / companion
2	
3	The goal: an assistant that knows the person's **life story** — people, places, history, plans,
4	preferences, how they're feeling — across many conversations, and updates that knowledge when
5	life changes. This lesson is the design; Lessons 9–10 build it.
6	
7	## What a companion needs to remember
8	
9	| Kind | Example | Lifetime | Why it matters |
10	|---|---|---|---|
11	| **fact** | "Alex's sister Maya is a nurse in Denver" | until it changes | biography |
12	| **preference** | "Alex likes quiet mornings and hates phone calls" | until it changes | personalization |
13	| **event** | "Alex's presentation was praised on 2026-11-12" | permanent, dated | life timeline |
14	| **plan** | "Maya visits for Thanksgiving on 2026-11-26" | open → done | proactive follow-ups |
15	| **feeling** | "Alex was nervous about the presentation" | fades within days | empathy, tone |
16	| **boundary** | "Don't bring up Alex's ex, Jordan" | until revoked | trust and safety |
17	
18	Plus two things that aren't single memories:
19	- **The life graph**: who and what is in their life and how they relate (sister, pet, employer).
20	- **Episodes**: each conversation, with a summary and mood, linked in order — the "diary".
21	
22	## Why graph + vectors (not just a vector store)
23	
24	| Need | Vectors alone | Graph + vectors |
25	|---|---|---|
26	| "How's my sister?" → find Maya | ✅ fuzzy match | ✅ alias "my sister" → Maya, then hop |
27	| Everything about Maya | ❌ only text that *looks* similar | ✅ `(m)-[:ABOUT]->(Maya)` |
28	| "I moved to Seattle" replaces "lives in Portland" | ❌ both stay, contradicting | ✅ `SUPERSEDES` + `invalidated_at` |
29	| What was true in March? | ❌ | ✅ bi-temporal properties |
30	| Life timeline, open plans | ❌ | ✅ ordered by `occurred_on` / `due_on` |
31	| Never surface the ex | ❌ | ✅ exclude entities a boundary is `ABOUT` |
32	| Where did this memory come from? | ❌ | ✅ `(m)-[:FROM]->(Episode)` |
33	
34	## The schema — [`companion/schema.py`](../companion/schema.py)
35	
36	```
37	(:User:Entity {id, name, kind:'self'})
38	      │ RELATED {type: sister|pet|works_at|lives_in…, since}
39	      ▼
40	(:Entity {id, user, name, kind, aliases[], summary, embedding})   person|pet|place|organization|activity|thing
41	      ▲ ABOUT
42	      │
43	(:Memory {id, user, text, kind, importance 1-10, embedding,
44	          occurred_on, due_on, status,                 ← domain time: when it happened / is due
45	          created_at, invalidated_at,                  ← system time: when we learned / un-learned it
46	          last_accessed, access_count})                ← usage, for recency and reinforcement
47	      │ SUPERSEDES ──► (:Memory)  older version
48	      │ FROM ──────► (:Episode {id, user, started_at, ended_at, summary, mood, embedding})
49	                                  │ NEXT ──► (:Episode)
50	                                  │ HAS_TURN ──► (:Turn {idx, role, text, at})
51	```
52	
53	Design choices, and where they come from in earlier lessons:
54	
55	- **Memory is a node, not a relationship** (Lesson 3.2): a memory connects to *several*
56	  entities, has its own properties, and other things point at it (`SUPERSEDES`, `FROM`).
57	- **Entities are shared nodes** (Lesson 3.1): "who else is in Alex's life?" is a hop, and
58	  aliases ("my sister", "Mom") resolve to one node.
59	- **`MERGE` everything that has identity** (Lesson 2): the same Maya across 100 conversations.
60	- **Two time axes**: `occurred_on`/`due_on` say when something is true in the person's life;
61	  `created_at`/`invalidated_at` say when the system learned or retired it. Old facts are
62	  **retired, not deleted**, so history survives ("Alex used to live in Portland").
63	- **`user` property on every node** scopes all queries and vector searches to one person.
64	- **Three vector indexes** (Lesson 5): `memory_vec`, `entity_vec`, `episode_vec` (384-dim,
65	  local `bge-small` model, no API key).
66	
67	## Design principles for companion memory
68	
69	1. **Write standalone memories.** "Alex's sister Maya is a nurse", never "she's a nurse" — each
70	   memory must make sense alone, years later. Same for dates: absolute, never "next Thursday".
71	2. **Update, don't accumulate.** New information supersedes old; duplicates reinforce.
72	3. **Importance and recency both matter.** Retrieval ranks by similarity, importance and how
73	   recently a memory was used; feelings decay in ~a week, facts over months.
74	4. **Proactivity comes from plans.** Open plans near their due date are always in context, so
75	   the companion asks "how did it go?" instead of waiting to be told.
76	5. **Boundaries are hard filters**, applied in the query (not just the prompt), and the
77	   boundary itself is always in context.
78	6. **The user owns their memory**: inspect (`/memories`, `/timeline`, `/people`), see history
79	   (`/history`), and **hard-delete** (`/forget`) — privacy beats provenance for explicit requests.
80	7. **Never invent.** The extractor records only what the user said or confirmed; the companion
81	   is told to ask rather than guess.
82	
83	## Create the schema
84	
85	```bash
86	.venv/bin/python -c "from neo4j import GraphDatabase; import config; from companion.schema import ensure_schema; \
87	d = GraphDatabase.driver(config.NEO4J_URI, auth=config.NEO4J_AUTH); ensure_schema(d); print('ok')"
88	```
89	
90	(`MemoryStore(...)` also runs it automatically.)
91	
92	```cypher
93	SHOW INDEXES YIELD name, type WHERE name IN ['memory_vec','entity_vec','episode_vec','memory_user_kind']
94	```

20	## LangGraph in one picture
21	
22	A LangGraph app is a **state machine**: a typed state, **nodes** (functions that return state
23	updates) and **edges** (which node runs next, possibly chosen by a function).
24	
25	```
26	START ──► agent ──(tool calls?)──► tools ──┐
27	            ▲                              │
28	            └──────────────────────────────┘
29	          (no tool calls) ──► END
30	```
31	
32	```python
33	g = StateGraph(MessagesState)                    # state = the message list
34	g.add_node("agent", agent)                       # LLM with tools bound
35	g.add_node("tools", ToolNode(TOOLS))             # runs whatever tools the LLM asked for
36	g.add_edge(START, "agent")
37	g.add_conditional_edges("agent", tools_condition)  # -> "tools" if tool calls, else END
38	g.add_edge("tools", "agent")
39	app = g.compile(checkpointer=InMemorySaver())    # remembers messages per thread_id
40	```
41	
42	The **checkpointer** is LangGraph's short-term memory: every turn on the same `thread_id`
43	sees the earlier messages. (Lessons 8–10 add *long-term* memory in Neo4j.)

5. **If user needs cURL/raw HTTP examples**, read from `curl/`.

### Language-Specific Feature Support

Every SDK language above supports both the beta Tool Runner and Managed Agents (beta) - Python (`@beta_tool` decorator), TypeScript (`betaZodTool` + Zod), Java (annotated classes), Go (`BetaToolRunner` in the `toolrunner` pkg), Ruby (`BaseTool` + `tool_runner`), C# (`BetaToolRunner` + raw JSON schema), PHP (`BetaRunnableTool` + `toolRunner()`); code entry points are in the Tool Use Patterns quick reference below. cURL is raw HTTP (no SDK features) and supports Managed Agents.

---

## Which Surface Should I Use?

> **Start simple.** Default to the simplest tier that meets your needs. Single API calls and workflows handle most use cases - only reach for agents when the task genuinely requires open-ended, model-driven exploration. "Simplest" means the least code you own: for a hosted, scheduled, or memory-backed agent, Managed Agents is usually the simplest option (no loop code, no state files, no scheduler), even though it's a bigger platform.

| Use Case                                        | Tier            | Recommended Surface       | Why                                                          |
| ----------------------------------------------- | --------------- | ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Classification, summarization, extraction, Q&A  | Single LLM call | **Claude API**            | One request, one response                                    |
| Batch processing or embeddings                  | Single LLM call | **Claude API**            | Specialized endpoints                                        |
| Multi-step pipelines with code-controlled logic | Workflow        | **Claude API + tool use** | You orchestrate the loop                                     |
| Custom agent with your own tools                | Agent           | **Claude API + tool use** | Maximum flexibility                                          |
| Server-managed stateful agent with workspace    | Agent           | **Managed Agents**        | Anthropic runs the loop and hosts the tool-execution sandbox |
| Persisted, versioned agent configs              | Agent           | **Managed Agents**        | Agents are stored objects; sessions pin to a version         |
| Long-running multi-turn agent with file mounts  | Agent           | **Managed Agents**        | Per-session containers, SSE event stream, Skills + MCP       |
| Agent that runs on a schedule (cron, "every night") | Agent       | **Managed Agents** - scheduled deployments | Deployments fire sessions autonomously; no client-side scheduler |
| One deliverable that must meet a quality bar ("until it's right") | Agent | **Managed Agents** - outcomes | A separate grader iterates the agent against your rubric until it passes |
| Agent work split across several agents | Agent | **Managed Agents** - dynamic workflows | Many agents in phases |

> **Note:** Managed Agents is the right choice when you want Anthropic to run the agent loop *and* host the container where tools execute - file ops, bash, code execution all run in the per-session workspace. If you want to host the compute yourself or run your own custom tool runtime, Claude API + tool use is the right choice - use the tool runner for the agentic loop - its per-turn hooks still give you approval gates, logging, error interception, and conditional execution (see `shared/tool-use-concepts.md`) - or the manual loop when you want to own the entire loop yourself.

> **Cloud-provider access.** **Claude Platform on AWS** is Anthropic-operated with same-day API parity - see `shared/claude-platform-on-aws.md` for client setup. **Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed)** is Anthropic-operated too (`shared/google-cloud-anthropic-managed.
