tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: small — keep workflows under 5 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter

Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

scope.description: Required with items: "first_task", "continuation" or "new_task" (see the tool description). Omit on advance / done / start updates.

session.description: When you delegated this step to a session you started: that session's short name (from start_session's result). The app shows its live state on the step.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available, or one your own work this turn made available; others are refused, and one that later stops being available is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and other answers), so do not guess. Offer commit, create_pr or verify only once the work the user asked for is done, not every turn. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Not now": a button, not a sentence. A click sends it to you as the user's answer. Never a go-ahead to commit: that is the commit app action. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments. Never repeat an offer the user passed over, as an app action, a reply or a question in your closing message, unless what it acts on has changed since or they bring it up.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'press_key' presses a hardware key 'count' times: return, delete (backspace), an arrow, select_all, undo or redo (a key also hides the on-screen keyboard); 'set_appearance' switches the device to light or dark mode; 'appearance' says which it is in; 'set_keyboard' shows or hides the on-screen keyboard (it appears only while a text field has focus, and 'press_key' and 'text' hide it again); 'rotate' turns the device a quarter turn left or right ('direction'); take a 'screenshot' after it and tap in that screenshot's frame, however it comes back; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

app_path.description: For 'launch': absolute path (no ~) to the built .app bundle (e.g. /Users/me/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/MyApp-abc123/Build/Products/Debug-iphonesimulator/MyApp.app).

device.description: Simulator name (e.g. 'iPhone 17 Pro') or UDID. Defaults to the simulator already attached, else the first booted one. The first use of a device asks the user for permission.

udid.description: Alias for 'device' (identical semantics: simulator name or UDID). Pass at most one of 'device' / 'udid'.

bundle_id.description: For 'launch': bundle identifier. If omitted, extracted from the .app's Info.plist.

points.description: For 'touch_path': touch path samples in device points. First point is touch-down; last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000 ms; the first sample's is skipped, so send 0 or omit it; at most 30 seconds in all).

points2.description: For 'touch2_path': two-finger path samples in device points. Each sample carries both contacts (x1/y1, x2/y2); first is touch-down, last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000 ms; the first sample's is skipped, so send 0 or omit it; at most 30 seconds in all).

duration.description: Seconds. For 'tap', >0.5 is a long-press. For 'swipe', the gesture duration (default 0.3).

text.description: For 'text': the string to type.

name.description: For 'button': hardware button to press.

key.description: For 'press_key': the key or edit command to press.

count.description: For 'press_key': how many times to press it, 1 to 20 (default 1).

state.description: For 'set_keyboard': 'show' or 'hide' the on-screen keyboard. For 'set_appearance': 'light' or 'dark'.

url.description: For 'open_url': URL or scheme to open in the simulator.

If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. p='docs/design-decisions.md'
s=open(p).read()
old="| **Separate graph DB + vector DB** |"
new="""| **Another property-graph DB** (Memgraph, FalkorDB, Amazon Neptune; embedded: LadybugDB) | Memgraph: in-memory speed and streaming; FalkorDB: Redis-based, low latency, used by Graphiti and Cognee; Neptune: managed on AWS with LPG and RDF; embedded: no server at all | most speak Cypher or openCypher, so the ideas here carry over, but GDS, APOC and vector-index details differ. Kuzu, the best-known embedded option, was archived in October 2025; LadybugDB is its maintained fork |
| **Separate graph DB + vector DB** |"""
assert old in s; s=s.replace(old,new,1)
old="| **Managed memory service** (Mem0, Zep, Letta, LangMem) | you want memory as a product, not a project | less control over identity, time, privacy rules and evaluation; see [Other systems](#how-other-memory-systems-choose) |"
new="""| **Memory framework or service** (Mem0, Zep, Letta, Cognee, LangMem, Neo4j Labs `neo4j-agent-memory`) | you want memory as a product, not a project | less control over identity, time, privacy rules and evaluation; see [Other systems](#how-other-memory-systems-choose) |
| **Cloud platform memory** (Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory, Vertex AI Agent Engine Memory Bank) | you already build agents on that cloud; extraction and consolidation are run for you | the provider's extraction rules and scopes; facts are a flat list searched by similarity, with no graph to traverse |
| **Files the agent edits** (Anthropic's memory tool, Letta's git-backed MemFS) | the agent should curate its own notes; humans can read and diff them | no index or graph: the agent finds things with file search, and quality depends on the model's discipline |"""
assert old in s; s=s.replace(old,new,1)
old="| **Microsoft GraphRAG** |"
new="""| **Cognee** | graph + vector + relational, pluggable backends (Neo4j, FalkorDB, Kuzu/LadybugDB…) | an ECL pipeline: *add*, *cognify* (extract a graph), optional *memify* enrichment | re-run the pipeline; enrichment infers new links | graph and vector search combined |
| **Neo4j Labs `neo4j-agent-memory`** | Neo4j: short-term (messages), long-term (a POLE+O entity graph), *reasoning* memory (decision traces) | extraction pipeline with deduplication | entity merge | Cypher tools, also as an MCP server; a Labs project, so no support guarantees |
| **Cloud memory services** (Bedrock AgentCore Memory, Vertex AI Memory Bank) | managed store of extracted memory records per scope (user, session) | the service, asynchronously, from stored conversation events | the service consolidates (Memory Bank asks Gemini to merge and resolve contradictions) | similarity search within one scope |
| **Files the agent edits** (Anthropic memory tool, Letta MemFS, OpenAI Agents SDK sessions for history only) | Markdown files, versioned with git in Letta's case | the agent, with file tools | edit in place, history in git | file search and reads, no vector index by default |
| **Microsoft GraphRAG** |"""
assert old in s; s=s.replace(old,new,1)
old="| **MemGPT / Letta** | in-context *core* memory blocks + *archival* store + *recall* (conversation history) store |"
new="| **MemGPT / Letta** | in-context *core* memory blocks + *archival* store + *recall* (conversation history) store; since 2026 optionally a git-backed file tree (MemFS) |"
assert old in s; s=s.replace(old,new,1)
old="""Letta's sleep-time agents and our background extractor plus `consolidate()` solve the same
problem: memory work that shouldn't slow down the reply."""
new="""Letta's sleep-time agents and our background extractor plus `consolidate()` solve the same
problem: memory work that shouldn't slow down the reply.

Neo4j's own Labs package is the closest *on the same database*. Its three layers map onto
ours: short-term messages ≈ the checkpointer plus `Episode` nodes, long-term entity graph ≈
the life graph, reasoning memory ≈ nothing here (we don't store the agent's own decision
traces; [Lesson 18](../lessons/18-seeing-memory-work.md)'s trace is shown, not stored).

The 2026 trend is in two directions at once: cloud platforms hide memory behind an API with
scopes and similarity search, while coding agents move memory into plain files the model edits.
Both drop the graph. Keep one when your questions are about *relationships and time*, which a
companion's are."""
assert old in s; s=s.replace(old,new,1)
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF
grep -n "Revisit when" docs/design-decisions.md | head -3; grep -n "^## Gaps\|^## .*gap\|^## " docs/design-decisions.md

content.content:
## Gaps: what this design does not cover

Honest limits, and what would fill each one:

| Gap | Risk | What would fill it |
|---|---|---|
| **Memory poisoning / prompt injection** (OWASP's 2026 Top 10 for agentic applications lists it as ASI06, memory and context poisoning) | Text the user (or a pasted document) says is stored, then returned in future prompts as trusted memory, and it outlives the session | Store provenance and source type; treat memory as data in the prompt; filter instruction-like text at write time; review high-impact memories |
| **Scale** | One `User` node becomes a supernode; one Neo4j instance; post-filtered vector search | Partition by user (D4); bucket edges by time; dedicated vector index per tenant; read replicas (Enterprise) |
| **Keyword retrieval** | Rare exact words missed by embeddings | Full-text index + rank fusion (D11) |
| **Reflection / insights** | No higher-level conclusions ("Alex is happier since moving") | Scheduled LLM reflection writing new `insight` memories with evidence links |
| **Procedural memory learning** | The companion doesn't learn *how* to talk to this person beyond boundaries | Store style feedback as memories that edit the persona prompt; review before applying |
| **Multimodal memory** | Photos, voice, documents | Embeddings for images/audio, `Media` nodes linked `ABOUT` entities |
| **Shared memory across people** | Two users who know the same Maya have two Mayas | Global entity layer with consent; cross-user resolution |
| **Erasure outside the graph** | Backups, logs, traces, LLM provider retention | Retention policies, log redaction, provider no-retention settings |
| **Cost control** | One extraction call per turn, one remote embedding call per recall | Cheaper extraction model (`LLM_EXTRACTION_MODEL`), batching, caching, skipping more small talk |
| **Benchmarks** | Our scenarios aren't comparable with other systems | Run LoCoMo / LongMemEval / BEAM-style suites |
| **Learned thresholds** | Hand-measured cut-offs per model | Collect labelled pairs from the trace UI and refit |
| **Non-English** | Role-name rules and regexes are English | Language-aware rules; multilingual embedding model (Qwen3 is multilingual) |

---

content.content:
The same term often has a precise academic meaning, a working meaning among practitioners,
and a looser one in product marketing ("marketecture"). None is wrong, but mixing them causes
most design arguments. The last column says where this repo stands.

| Term | Academic / standards meaning | Practitioner meaning | Loose / marketing meaning | This repo |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Agent memory** | Long-term stores an agent reads and writes during its decision cycle (CoALA) | Persisting facts about users across sessions, plus retrieval into the prompt | Any feature that makes a chatbot "remember you"; "infinite memory", "perfect recall" | The practitioner meaning, with the psychology kinds made explicit (Lesson 8) |
| **Memory layer** | — (not an academic term) | A service between the app and the LLM that extracts, stores and retrieves memories (Mem0, Zep) | "Add memory to any agent in 3 lines" | A library-sized memory layer you can read end to end (`MemoryStore`) |
| **Context engineering** | Generalizes "context" from HCI (Dey); framed in 2025 papers as assembling the model's input | Choosing which tokens go into each call: instructions, tools, retrieved data, memory, history. The term spread in mid-2025 (Cognition, Shopify's CEO, Anthropic's September 2025 guide) | A rebrand of prompt engineering | `recall()` + `format_context()` + the trace that shows the result (Lessons 10, 18) |
| **Knowledge graph** | Entities and typed relations, usually under an ontology, often with reasoning (KR, Semantic Web) | A property graph of entities and facts used for search or RAG | Any graph database, or any data with links | Life graph + memories + RelType ontology ([knowledge graph](#knowledge-graph)) |
| **Temporal / bi-temporal KG** | Facts with valid time, and with transaction time too (temporal databases) | Facts that expire or get superseded instead of overwritten (Graphiti) | "Memory that understands time" | Bi-temporal memories and relations (Lessons 8, 13) |
| **Context graph** | — (a 2025–26 industry term) | A graph of *decisions*: policies, exceptions, precedents, evidence and outcomes, so agents know *why* something happened. Thoughtworks' Radar (April 2026) rates it "Assess" | The next thing after knowledge graphs | Partly: provenance (`FROM` episode), supersession history and the trace record what was *said* and *decided by the code*, but not decisions with reasons as nodes |
| **Ontology** | OWL/RDFS classes, properties and axioms with formal semantics | A typed vocabulary with rules shared by a team | Palantir's *Ontology*: an operational layer of business objects, links **and actions** that apps and agents act through; or any data model | A lightweight ontology (sense 2 under [ontology](#ontology)), no actions |
| **Semantic layer** | — (BI and data-warehouse term) | Governed definitions of metrics and dimensions over a warehouse (dbt, Snowflake semantic models, LookML) | "The semantic layer for AI": any metadata an agent can read | Not used. The ontology plays the "agreed meaning" role for relation types |
| **GraphRAG** | Microsoft Research's method (2024): an entity graph plus community summaries for global questions; later DRIFT and LazyGraphRAG | Any RAG that retrieves through a graph, usually vector entry points + traversal | "RAG, but with a graph, so no hallucinations" | The local style (Lessons 5, 10) |
| **Hybrid search** | Lexical (BM25) + dense retrieval, fused (e.g. reciprocal-rank fusion) | Same, or vector + graph | "Best of both worlds" | Vector + graph; no lexical retriever yet ([D11](design-decisions.md#d11)) |
| **Vector database** | — | A database built around ANN indexes (Pinecone, Qdrant, Milvus...) | Anything with a vector index, including general databases | A vector index inside Neo4j ([D1](design-decisions.md#d1)) |
| **Agentic RAG** | — | The model decides when and what to retrieve, in a loop, through tools | Any RAG with an LLM involved | Lesson 7 is agentic; the companion's recall is not ([D10](design-decisions.md#d10)) |
| **Reranking** | Re-scoring a candidate list with a stronger model (cross-encoder, learning to rank) | Same, often a hosted reranker API | — | A formula plus an optional cross-encoder label ([rerank and relevance](#rerank-and-relevance)) |
| **Consolidation / sleep-time compute** | Memory consolidation in neuroscience (sleep strengthens and reorganizes memories) | Background jobs that rewrite memory between conversations (Letta's sleep-time agents) | "Your agent learns while it sleeps" | End-of-episode pass + `consolidate()` (Lessons 11, 13) |
| **Memory poisoning** | Data poisoning / prompt injection research applied to stored memory | Malicious or mistaken text stored as memory and trusted later; ASI06 in OWASP's 2026 Top 10 for agentic applications | — | A known gap ([gaps](design-decisions.md#gaps-what-this-design-does-not-cover)) |
| **Long-term memory benchmark** | Datasets with defined tasks: LoCoMo (2024), LongMemEval (2024: adds knowledge updates and abstention), BEAM (2026: 1M–10M tokens) | Leaderboard numbers on those | Self-reported scores across vendors, often with different settings | Not run; our scenarios are code-graded and repo-specific ([D20](design-decisions.md#d20)) |
| **Digital twin** | A simulation model kept in sync with a physical system | A live model of an organization's entities and processes | Any database about real things | Not used |

**How to read a vendor claim:**
1. Ask which **sense** of the word is meant, using the table above.
Only (1) and (4) remove data.

### instruction

(1) a **system prompt** or persona instruction to the chat model; (2) an embedding model's
**query instruction**: text put before a query so the model embeds it for retrieval
(Lesson 19); (3) instruction-tuned models in general. Sense 2 is never seen by the chat model.

"""Lesson 19 — the companion's embedding model: where it runs, and the thresholds measured for it.

Every similarity cut-off in the memory store (is this a duplicate? the same person? part of a
habit?) was measured on ONE model's scores. Another model spreads its scores differently, so
switching models without re-measuring silently breaks dedupe, entity matching and recall.
A Profile keeps a model and its thresholds together:

    local   BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5    384 dims, on the CPU via fastembed, no key   (default)
    remote  Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-8B   4096 dims, any OpenAI-compatible /embeddings endpoint

Each model's vectors live in their own property and vector indexes ("embedding" + memory_vec
for the default, "embedding_qwen3_embedding_8b" + memory_vec_qwen3_embedding_8b for Qwen), so
one database can hold both: the tests run on the local model while your chats use the remote
one, and `python -m companion.reembed` backfills a model's vectors after a switch.

Queries vs passages: Qwen3-Embedding is trained to put an instruction before a QUERY ("what
does this message relate to?") and nothing before a stored text. Without it, its separation
of related from unrelated memories fell from 0.99 to 0.90 AUC (lessons/19). So `embed(...,
query=True)` is for a message searched against memories; comparisons between two stored
things (memory vs memory, entity vs entity) use plain embeddings on both sides.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import re
import threading
from collections import OrderedDict
from dataclasses import dataclass

import numpy as np

import config


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Profile:
    model: str
    dims: int
    # Thresholds. "score" = the vector index's 0-1 score, (1 + cosine) / 2; "cosine" = raw.
    duplicate: float          # score: a new memory this close to a current one reinforces it
    forgotten: float          # cosine: this close to a /forget tombstone is not stored again
    entity_match: float       # score: an entity this close (same kind) may be the same one...
    name_match: float         # cosine: ...if their NAMES are this close too ("Mom" ~ "my mother")
    pattern: float            # cosine: every pair in a habit cluster at least this close
    sensitive_floor: float    # score: a sensitive memory needs at least this to be recalled
    sensitive_margin: float   # score: ...and to be within this of the best match
    entity_hop: float         # score: an entity this close to the message is looked up
    query_instruction: str = ""    # put before a query (not before stored text)
    cluster_instruction: str = ""  # put before memories grouped into habits (Lesson 13)
    # score: below this a vector match is "loosely related" (Lesson 18). None: the model can't
    # tell (bge-small's scores overlap), so a cross-encoder decides instead.
    weak_below: float | None = None

    @property
    def slug(self) -> str:
        """'' for the default model (the property and index names from Lessons 8-18)."""
        if self.model == DEFAULT_MODEL:
            return ""
        return re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9]+", "_", self.model.split("/")[-1].lower()).strip("_")

    @property
    def prop(self) -> str:
        return f"embedding_{self.slug}" if self.slug else "embedding"

    def index(self, base: str) -> str:
        return f"{base}_{self.slug}" if self.slug else base


DEFAULT_MODEL = config.LOCAL_EMBED_MODEL

PROFILES = {p.model: p for p in [
    # Lessons 9-13 measured these (see the comments next to each constant in store.py).
    Profile("BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5", dims=384, duplicate=0.975, forgotten=0.90, entity_match=0.93,
            name_match=0.80, pattern=0.82, sensitive_floor=0.72, sensitive_margin=0.01, entity_hop=0.85),
    # Lesson 19: measured with `python -m companion.calibrate` (results in the lesson).
    # Its scores spread wider than bge-small's: unrelated pairs sit lower (sensitive/hop "no"
    # 0.57-0.62 vs bge's 0.68-0.74), so the floors drop, and a message that only MEANS an
    # entity ("how is my kid doing?" -> Logan) now clears the hop (0.65-0.73 vs no <= 0.59).
    Profile("Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-8B", dims=4096, duplicate=0.966, forgotten=0.89, entity_match=0.94,
            name_match=0.84, pattern=0.665, sensitive_floor=0.655, sensitive_margin=0.015, entity_hop=0.62,
            query_instruction="Instruct: Given a message from a user, retrieve memories about the "
                              "user's life that it relates to\nQuery: ",
            # without it, "heading to the gym" vs "went rock climbing" (0.77) outscored two
            # gym sentences (0.73): complete-linkage clustering couldn't find the habit
            cluster_instruction="Instruct: Identify the activity or habit described\nQuery: ",
            # one cut on the best match got 36 of 37 test messages right (raw cosine 0.312)
            weak_below=0.656),
]}


def profile_for(model: str) -> Profile:
    if model not in PROFILES:
        raise SystemExit(
            f"No thresholds measured for EMBED_MODEL={model!r}. Add a Profile for it in "
            "companion/embeddings.py, measured with `python -m companion.calibrate` (Lesson 19).")
    return PROFILES[model]


PROFILE = profile_for(config.EMBED_MODEL)

_local = None
_client = None
_lock = threading.Lock()
_cache: OrderedDict[tuple[str, str], np.ndarray] = OrderedDict()  # (instruction, text) -> unit vector
CACHE_SIZE = 2048  # names and summaries are embedded again and again during one extraction


def remote() -> bool:
    return bool(config.EMBED_BASE_URL)


def _compute(texts: list[str]) -> np.ndarray:
    global _local, _client
    if not remote():
        if _local is None:
            from fastembed import TextEmbedding
            _local = TextEmbedding(PROFILE.model)
        return np.array(list(_local.embed(texts)), dtype=np.float32)
    if _client is None:
        from openai import OpenAI
        _client = OpenAI(base_url=config.EMBED_BASE_URL, api_key=REDACTED, timeout=60, max_retries=3)
    out = []
    for i in range(0, len(texts), 64):  # endpoints cap the batch size
        resp = _client.embeddings.create(model=PROFILE.model, input=texts[i:i + 64], encoding_format="float")
        out += [d.embedding for d in sorted(resp.data, key=lambda d: d.index)]
    vecs = np.array(out, dtype=np.float32)
    if vecs.shape[1] != PROFILE.dims:
        raise RuntimeError(f"{PROFILE.model} returned {vecs.shape[1]} dims, expected {PROFILE.dims}")
    return vecs


def embed(texts: list[str], query: bool = False) -> list[list[float]]:
    """Unit-length vectors (so a dot product is the cosine). `query=True`: the text is a message
    searched against stored memories/entities, and gets the model's query instruction."""
    return _embed(texts, PROFILE.query_instruction if query else "")


def embed_for_clustering(texts: list[str]) -> list[list[float]]:
    """Vectors for grouping memories into habits. Not stored: consolidation embeds again
    when the model has a clustering instruction, else it can use the stored vectors."""
    return _embed(texts, PROFILE.cluster_instruction)


def _embed(texts: list[str], instruction: str) -> list[list[float]]:
    keys = [(instruction, t) for t in texts]
    found: dict[tuple[str, str], np.ndarray] = {}
    with _lock:
        for k in keys:
            if k in _cache:
                found[k] = _cache[k]
                _cache.move_to_end(k)
    missing = [k for k in dict.fromkeys(keys) if k not in found]
    if missing:
        vecs = _compute([i + t for i, t in missing])
        vecs /= np.linalg.norm(vecs, axis=1, keepdims=True)
        found.update(zip(missing, vecs))
        with _lock:
            _cache.update(zip(missing, vecs))
            while len(_cache) > CACHE_SIZE:
                _cache.popitem(last=False)
    return [found[k].tolist() for k in keys]
"""Lesson 19 — give every stored memory, entity and episode a vector from the active model.

    python -m companion.reembed              nodes that don't have one yet (after a switch)
    python -m companion.reembed --all        recompute every vector (e.g. a changed instruction)
    python -m companion.reembed --user Mark  one user only

Run it after changing EMBED_MODEL / EMBED_BASE_URL. Each model writes its own property
(embedding / embedding_<model>), so the old vectors stay and switching back costs nothing.
The text embedded is the same text the write path embeds (keep them in step: a vector made
from different text matches differently). Tombstones (:Forgotten) keep no text, so they
can't be re-embedded; they only matter while their episode is open, so that's harmless.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import sys
import time

from neo4j import GraphDatabase

from config import NEO4J_AUTH, NEO4J_URI
from companion.embeddings import PROFILE, embed, remote
from companion.schema import ensure_schema

# label -> Cypher for the text the write path embeds for it (store.py)
TEXTS = {
    "User": "n.name + ', the user'",
    "Entity": "n.name + ' (' + n.kind + '): ' + coalesce(n.summary, '')",
    "Memory": "n.text",
    "Episode": "n.summary",
}
BATCH = 64


def reembed(driver, user: str | None = None, everything: bool = False) -> dict[str, int]:
    """`user`: a user's name ("Mark"), as MemoryStore takes it; None for everyone."""
    user = f"user:{user.lower()}" if user else None  # the id MemoryStore gives that user
    ensure_schema(driver)  # this model's vector indexes
    counts = {}
    for label, text in TEXTS.items():
        where = ["n[$prop] IS NULL"] if not everything else []
        where += [f"{text} IS NOT NULL"]
        if label == "Entity":
            where.append("NOT n:User")
        if user:
            where.append("n.user = $user")
        rows, _, _ = driver.execute_query(
            f"MATCH (n:{label}) WHERE {' AND '.join(where)} RETURN elementId(n) AS id, {text} AS text",
            prop=PROFILE.prop, user=user)
        for i in range(0, len(rows), BATCH):
            chunk = rows[i:i + BATCH]
            vecs = embed([r["text"] for r in chunk])
            driver.execute_query(
                """
                UNWIND $rows AS row MATCH (n) WHERE elementId(n) = row.id
                CALL db.create.setNodeVectorProperty(n, $prop, row.vec)
                """,
                rows=[{"id": r["id"], "vec": v} for r, v in zip(chunk, vecs)], prop=PROFILE.prop)
        counts[label] = len(rows)
    return counts


def main() -> None:
    args = sys.argv[1:]
    user = args[args.index("--user") + 1] if "--user" in args else None
    where = f"{PROFILE.model} via {'the endpoint in EMBED_BASE_URL' if remote() else 'fastembed (local)'}"
    print(f"Embedding with {where} -> property {PROFILE.prop}")
    start = time.time()
    with GraphDatabase.driver(NEO4J_URI, auth=NEO4J_AUTH) as driver:
        counts = reembed(driver, user, everything="--all" in args)
    print(", ".join(f"{n} {label.lower()}" for label, n in counts.items()), f"in {time.time() - start:.1f}s")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

    "Episode": "n.summary",
}
BATCH = 64


def reembed(driver, user: str | None = None, everything: bool = False) -> dict[str, int]:
    """`user`: a user's name ("Mark"), as MemoryStore takes it; None for everyone."""
    user = f"user:{user.lower()}" if user else None  # the id MemoryStore gives that user
    ensure_schema(driver)  # this model's vector indexes
    counts = {}
    for label, text in TEXTS.items():
        where = ["n[$prop] IS NULL"] if not everything else []
        where += [f"{text} IS NOT NULL"]
        if label == "Entity":
            where.append("NOT n:User")
        if user:
            where.append("n.user = $user")
        rows, _, _ = driver.execute_query(
            f"MATCH (n:{label}) WHERE {' AND '.join(where)} RETURN elementId(n) AS id, {text} AS text",
            prop=PROFILE.prop, user=user)
        for i in range(0, len(rows), BATCH):
            chunk = rows[i:i + BATCH]
            vecs = embed([r["text"] for r in chunk])
            driver.execute_query(
                """
                UNWIND $rows AS row MATCH (n) WHERE elementId(n) = row.id
                CALL db.create.setNodeVectorProperty(n, $prop, row.vec)
                """,
                rows=[{"id": r["id"], "vec": v} for r, v in zip(chunk, vecs)], prop=PROFILE.prop)
        counts[label] = len(rows)
    return counts


def main() -> None:
    args = sys.argv[1:]
    user = args[args.index("--user") + 1] if "--user" in args else None
    where = f"{PROFILE.model} via {'the endpoint in EMBED_BASE_URL' if remote() else 'fastembed (local)'}"
    print(f"Embedding with {where} -> property {PROFILE.prop}")
    start = time.time()
    with GraphDatabase.driver(NEO4J_URI, auth=NEO4J_AUTH) as driver:
        counts = reembed(driver, user, everything="--all" in args)
    print(", ".join(f"{n} {label.lower()}" for label, n in counts.items()), f"in {time.time() - start:.1f}s")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

1:# Neo4j graph tutorial
7:## Quick start
18:## For architects of agent memory
43:## Lessons
71:## LLM settings (lessons 5 and 7–19)
101:## Files
127:## Tests and evals
144:## Common commands
## Where to go next

Later lessons build on this:
- **[Lesson 11](11-harder-scenarios-and-evals.md)**: scripted conversations with known facts as
  evals, checking recall and whether boundaries ever leak.
- **[Lesson 12](12-ontology.md)**: a relation ontology (synonyms, one-at-a-time relations,
  inferred family links).
- **[Lesson 13](13-memory-over-time.md)**: expiry, decay, and a consolidation job that rolls
  repeated memories up into habits and prunes faded trivia.

- **[Lesson 14](14-production-hardening.md)**: transactions, a lock against duplicate writes,
  and extraction in the background so replies never wait on it.
- **[Lesson 15](15-graph-embeddings.md)**: graph embeddings (`gds.fastRP`) on the life graph to
  find related people and themes.
- **[Lesson 16](16-personas.md)**: several personas with their own view of the same person.
- **[Lesson 17](17-web-ui.md)**: a web page showing the chat, the graph and the decay curves.
=== lessons/00-setup.md
```

> The lessons build on each other: later outputs assume you ran the earlier lessons' write
> queries in order. Outputs recorded here are from the original run on 2026-11-05.
=== lessons/01-graph-basics-and-reading.md
- **Return nodes, relationships or paths** to get a picture; return values to get a table.
- **Patterns are the query.** Arrows can point either way, or meet in the middle `->(s)<-`.
- **Hops are cheap.** `*1..3` and `shortestPath` replace recursive SQL.
- **`WITH`** joins query stages into a pipeline; use it to filter on aggregates.
=== lessons/02-writing-data.md
| Enforce uniqueness | `CREATE CONSTRAINT ... REQUIRE n.k IS UNIQUE` |
| Speed up lookups | `CREATE INDEX ... FOR (n:Label) ON (n.k)` |
| Bulk load | `UNWIND $rows AS row MERGE ...` |
| Delete a node | `DELETE` (fails if it has relationships) or `DETACH DELETE` |
=== lessons/03-modeling-and-performance.md
| Groups/tags nodes cheaply | **Extra label** (`:Mentor`) |

Performance: avoid **AllNodesScan** / **NodeByLabelScan + Filter**; aim for **IndexSeek**;
index start points; use `$parameters`.
=== lessons/04-graph-algorithms-and-python.md
| Clusters | `gds.louvain` (also `gds.wcc`, `gds.labelPropagation`) |
| "Similar to" | `gds.nodeSimilarity`, `gds.knn` |
| Paths | `gds.shortestPath.dijkstra`, `gds.allShortestPaths` |
| Clean up | `CALL gds.graph.drop('name')` |
=== lessons/05-vectors-and-graphrag.md
| Store a vector | `CALL db.create.setNodeVectorProperty(n, 'embedding', $vec)` |
| Index it | `CREATE VECTOR INDEX ... OPTIONS {indexConfig: {`vector.dimensions`: N, `vector.similarity_function`: 'cosine'}}` |
| Search | `CALL db.index.vector.queryNodes('index', k, $vec) YIELD node, score` |
| GraphRAG | vector search → `MATCH (node)-[r]-(other)` → facts → LLM |
=== lessons/07-langgraph-agent-with-graph-tools.md

- Start with **fixed, parameterized tools**; add free-form Cypher behind a read-only transaction.
- Put the **schema in the tool description** so the model can write queries.
- LangGraph's checkpointer gives **short-term** memory per thread; long-term memory needs a store.
=== lessons/08-memory-design-for-companions.md

Schema setup must be idempotent, so the test runs `ensure_schema()` **twice** and then checks
that every constraint and vector index is `ONLINE`. A second test proves the id constraint
actually rejects a duplicate.
=== lessons/09-memory-write-path.md
```
2026-11-05T12:00Z, 8, TRUE
2026-11-13T12:00Z, 6, FALSE
```
=== lessons/11-harder-scenarios-and-evals.md
- Small embedding models compress scores: prefer relative thresholds.
- Test memory with multi-session scenarios that check both the graph and the replies, and read the transcripts.

Next: [Lesson 12 — an ontology for the life graph](12-ontology.md) replaces the hand-written relation groups with a real vocabulary and rules.
=== lessons/12-ontology.md
- **Infer** at read time when facts change often; materialize only when queries need the speed.
- When a step "does nothing", print the raw LLM output before blaming the LLM.

Next: [Lesson 13 — memory over time](13-memory-over-time.md): expiry, decay and consolidation.
```

- **Patterns are the query.** Arrows can point either way, or meet in the middle `->(s)<-`.
- **Hops are cheap.** `*1..3` and `shortestPath` replace recursive SQL.
- **`WITH`** joins query stages into a pipeline; use it to filter on aggregates.
+## Next
+[Lesson 2](02-writing-data.md) changes the graph: `CREATE`, `MERGE`, `SET` and `DELETE`, and the constraints that keep it clean.
+[← Lesson 0: Setup](00-setup.md) · [All lessons](../README.md#lessons) · [Lesson 2: Writing data →](02-writing-data.md)
| Speed up lookups | `CREATE INDEX ... FOR (n:Label) ON (n.k)` |
| Bulk load | `UNWIND $rows AS row MERGE ...` |
| Delete a node | `DELETE` (fails if it has relationships) or `DETACH DELETE` |
+## Next

+[Lesson 3](03-modeling-and-performance.md) asks how to *shape* the graph (node, relationship or property?) and how to make queries fast. Its reification pattern is how memories are modeled in Lesson 8.

index start points; use `$parameters`.

| Clean up | `CALL gds.graph.drop('name')` |

import re, glob, os
def slug(h):
    h = re.sub(r"[`*_]|\[|\]\([^)]*\)", "", h.strip().lower()) if False else h.strip().lower()
    h = re.sub(r"\]\([^)]*\)", "", h); h = h.replace("[","")
    h = re.sub(r"[^\w\- ]", "", h); return h.replace(" ", "-")
anchors = {}
files = glob.glob('lessons/*.md') + glob.glob('docs/*.md') + ['README.md']
for f in files:
    a=set(); seen={}
    incode=False
    for line in open(f):
        if line.startswith("```"): incode = not incode
        if incode: continue
        m = re.match(r"#{1,6} (.*)", line)
        if m:
            s = slug(m.group(1)); n = seen.get(s,0); seen[s]=n+1
            a.add(s if n==0 else f"{s}-{n}")
        a.update(re.findall(r'<a id="([^"]+)"', line))
    anchors[os.path.normpath(f)] = a
bad=0; total=0
for f in files:
    text = re.sub(r"```.*?```", "", open(f).read(), flags=re.S)
    for t in re.findall(r"\]\(([^)\s]+)\)", text):
        if t.startswith(("http","mailto:")): continue
        total+=1
        path, _, frag = t.partition("#")
        tgt = os.path.normpath(os.path.join(os.path.dirname(f), path)) if path else os.path.normpath(f)
        if not os.path.exists(tgt): print("MISSING", f, t); bad+=1; continue
        if frag and tgt.endswith(".md") and frag not in anchors.get(tgt,set()): print("ANCHOR", f, t); bad+=1
print("links", total, "bad", bad)
EOF

content.text:
I finished the fact-check, the code and design review, and the lesson-flow review, and verified the links. All 197 tests pass (the 42 that need a live LLM weren't run). Nothing is committed.

**Fact-check: the alternatives are now current to November 2026**
- **Design decisions, D1 alternatives:** I added three options:
  - **Other graph databases:** Memgraph, FalkorDB, Neptune, and LadybugDB for embedded use. Kuzu was archived in October 2025, and LadybugDB is its maintained fork.
  - **Cloud memory services:** Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory and Vertex AI Memory Bank.
  - **Memory kept as files:** Anthropic's memory tool and Letta's git-backed file memory, MemFS.
- **"How other memory systems choose":** new rows for Cognee, Neo4j Labs' `neo4j-agent-memory`, the cloud services, and file-based memory. The Letta row now mentions MemFS. A short note says where the field is heading: cloud services and file-based memory both leave out the graph.
- **Gaps:** added "reasoning memory", meaning stored traces of the agent's own decisions. Neo4j Labs' package has this and our design doesn't.
- **Glossary:** three new terms (reasoning memory, cloud memory bank, memory as files) and nine new sources.
- **Lesson 9:** the Mem0 row was out of date. It now says the LLM picks ADD/UPDATE/DELETE in Mem0 1.x, while Mem0 2.0 only adds and resolves conflicts when reading.
- **Lesson 7:** now mentions LangChain 1.0's `create_agent` and the Postgres checkpointer.
- **README and Lesson 8:** their lists of alternatives match the design doc.

**Code review**
I ran a linter and read the recently changed code.
- **Fixed in `companion/embeddings.py`:**
  - The local model or API client could be created twice when the background extractor and the chat started at the same moment. Creation now happens under a lock.
  - An all-zero vector caused a divide-by-zero. It is now guarded.
- **Fixed in the tests:** an unused import in `tests/test_19_embeddings.py`.
- **Left as they are:**
  - The broad `except Exception` blocks are deliberate fallbacks so memory extraction never breaks the chat.
  - The loop-variable lambda in consolidation runs immediately, so it's safe.
  - The web page escapes every piece of text it inserts, and the server listens only on 127.0.0.1.

**Educational flow and links**
- Lessons 0–5 and 7–9 had no "Next" section, and Lesson 10's list stopped at Lesson 17. Every lesson now ends with a "## Next" section that leads into the next lesson's story.

content.text:
No, I wouldn't require remote embeddings everywhere, but the companion should use the larger model by default. And the tests aren't fully up to date: most of them assume the small local model, and 10 fail on Qwen.

**What I measured.** I ran the full suite against Qwen3-Embedding-8B. 187 of 197 tests pass, compared with 197 of 197 on the small local model, bge-small. The 10 failures:

- **Nine assume bge-small.** They hard-code its numbers or behaviour:
  - the 0.975 duplicate cut-off (`test_18` ×2);
  - the cross-encoder's relevance labels (`test_10` ×2, `test_19` weak labels);
  - the local calibration pairs and the default `embedding` property name (`test_19` ×3);
  - one clustering test (`test_13`), where Qwen puts a fourth gym sentence in the group.
  
  None of these show a problem in Qwen's results. The tests just don't account for the model.
- **One is a real quality difference.** Qwen scores "Bob" vs "Robert" at 0.837, just under its 0.84 name-match cut-off, so "Bob" isn't kept as an alias. Lesson 19 already calls this a tradeoff: Qwen gets 10 of 13 name pairs right, and nicknames usually come from the extractor anyway.
- **The LLM evals run on bge-small too.** `pytest -m llm` uses the same pinning, so only the scenarios (53/53 earlier) currently test the model your chats use.

**Why not remote everywhere:**
- Lessons 5–7 and the default test run should stay local: they work offline, need no key, give the same results every run, and you can watch every step.
- If everything were remote, you'd need a key and network for every test run. The provider could also change the model and move scores without anyone noticing.
- Mixing models is safe: each model's vectors live in their own property and index.

**What I'd change:**
1. **Recommend remote for the companion.** It already needs an LLM endpoint, and DeepInfra serves Qwen from the same endpoint. So `.env.example` and the README would present `EMBED_BASE_URL` as the normal setup, with local as the offline fallback.
2. **Make the tests model-aware.**
   - Tests that check a threshold would read it from the active model's thresholds instead of a typed number.
   - The few tests that really are about bge-small (its cross-encoder labels, its calibration pairs) would be skipped on the remote model, with a reason.
   - The Bob/Robert test would give "Bob" as an alias, the way the extractor does.
   - Then `TEST_REMOTE_EMBEDDINGS=1 pytest` should pass completely on Qwen.
3. **Add a documented "release check":** the full suite, the LLM evals and the scenarios, all on the remote model. Default `pytest` stays local and fast.

Nothing is changed or committed yet, including last turn's review edits. Should I do both 1 and 2 (with 3 in the docs), or only make the tests model-aware?

"""Lesson 10 — recall and chat. Deterministic parts first (the small-talk gate, recall
queries, the prompt block); how the LLM *uses* the memories is graded in test_11."""
import datetime as dt

import pytest

from companion.graph import worth_remembering
from companion.models import EntityOut, Extraction, MemoryOut, RelationOut
from companion.store import format_context

T = dt.date(2026, 11, 5)


@pytest.mark.parametrize("text,expected", [
    ("ok", False), ("haha yeah", False), ("Thanks!", False), ("good night", False),
    ("ok so my sister is moving to Denver", True),
    ("My dog Rex is sick", True),
    ("no", False),
])
def test_small_talk_gate(text, expected):
        entities=[EntityOut(name="Maya", kind="person"), EntityOut(name="Rex", kind="pet")],
        relations=[RelationOut(source="user", target="Maya", type="sister"),
                   RelationOut(source="user", target="Rex", type="pet")],
        memories=[m("Pytest's sister Maya is a nurse in Denver", about=["Maya"]),
                  m("Pytest's dog Rex is afraid of thunderstorms", about=["Rex"]),
                  m("Pytest doesn't want to talk about their job", "boundary", importance=9),
                  m("Pytest is being treated for anxiety", sensitive=True, importance=8),
                  m("Pytest has a job interview at Acme", "plan", due_on="2026-11-06")],
    ), today=T)
    return store


def test_semantic_recall_finds_the_right_memory(life):
    r = life.recall("how is your sister doing?", today=T)
    texts = [x["text"] for x in r["semantic"]] + [x["text"] for e in r["entities"] for x in e["memories"]]
    assert "Pytest's sister Maya is a nurse in Denver" in texts


def test_an_unrelated_message_gets_only_loosely_related_memories(life):
    """Vector search always returns its nearest memories: "do you like pizza?" still scores
    about 0.7 against the dog and the sister (found in the web UI). The reranker labels them
    for the trace. They're not dropped: inferential matches score just as low."""
    r = life.recall("do you like pizza?", today=T)
    assert r["semantic"] and all(x["weak"] and x["relevance"] < -8.5 for x in r["semantic"])


def test_a_related_message_keeps_its_match_on_top(life):
    r = life.recall("my dog hates storms", today=T)
    top = r["semantic"][0]
    assert top["text"] == "Pytest's dog Rex is afraid of thunderstorms" and not top["weak"]


def test_an_inferential_match_is_kept_even_when_the_reranker_misses_it(store):
    """"My meds don't help" -> the ADHD memory: the reranker scores it like noise (-10.9),
    so dropping weak matches would hide exactly this (the sensitive scenario caught it)."""
    store.apply(Extraction(memories=[m("Pytest was diagnosed with ADHD in 2025 and takes medication for it",
                                       sensitive=True)]), today=T)
    r = store.recall("I'm struggling to focus at work, my meds don't seem to help", today=T)
    assert "ADHD" in format_context(r, T)
    assert r["semantic"][0]["weak"]  # the reranker did miss it: only the vector search found it


def test_boundaries_are_always_in_core(life):
    r = life.recall("what should I cook tonight?", today=T)
    assert any("doesn't want to talk about their job" in x["text"] for x in r["core"])


def test_sensitive_memories_stay_out_of_core(life):
    r = life.recall("what should I cook tonight?", today=T)
    assert not any("anxiety" in x["text"] for x in r["core"])


def test_followups_include_upcoming_plans(life):
    # Regression: the "job" boundary is ABOUT the user, and used to hide every memory
    # about the user, this plan included.
    r = life.recall("hi", today=T)

import datetime as dt

from test_17_web import D1, client, wait_for_memories  # noqa: F401  (client is a fixture)

from companion.embeddings import PROFILE
from companion.models import EntityOut, Extraction, MemoryOut, RelationOut

"""Lesson 19 — choosing an embedding model: profiles, query instructions, re-embedding.

    .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/test_19_embeddings.py -v

These run on the local model (conftest.py sets that up), and a fake endpoint stands in for the
remote one, so they check the wiring without an API key. Whether a remote model's thresholds
are RIGHT is what `python -m companion.calibrate` and the scenarios measure.
"""
import numpy as np
import pytest

from companion import calibrate, embeddings
from companion.embeddings import PROFILES, embed, profile_for
from companion.models import Extraction, MemoryOut
from companion.schema import vector_indexes

QWEN = PROFILES["Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-8B"]


def test_the_default_model_keeps_the_names_lessons_8_to_18_use():
    local = profile_for("BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5")
    assert (local.prop, local.index("memory_vec")) == ("embedding", "memory_vec")
    assert embeddings.PROFILE == local  # conftest: the tests run on the local model


def test_another_model_gets_its_own_property_and_indexes():
    assert QWEN.prop == "embedding_qwen3_embedding_8b"
    stmts = " ".join(vector_indexes(QWEN))
    assert "memory_vec_qwen3_embedding_8b" in stmts and "n.embedding_qwen3_embedding_8b" in stmts
    assert "`vector.dimensions`: 4096" in stmts  # an index has ONE size: 384 and 4096 can't share

def test_vectors_are_unit_length_and_cached(fake_remote):
    a = embed(["Mom", "Mom", "mother"])
    assert fake_remote == [["Mom", "mother"]]  # one call, each text once
    assert embed(["mother"]) == [a[2]] and len(fake_remote) == 1  # from the cache
    assert embed(["mother"], query=True) and len(fake_remote) == 2  # a query is a different vector
    assert all(abs(np.linalg.norm(v) - 1) < 1e-6 for v in a)


def test_clustering_uses_its_own_instruction(fake_remote):
    embeddings.embed_for_clustering(["Riley is at the gym"])
    assert fake_remote[0][0].startswith("Instruct: Identify the activity")


def test_the_local_thresholds_hold_on_the_calibration_pairs():
    """The pairs calibrate.py measures a new model on also pin down the current one. These
    three thresholds decide alone; entity matching and sensitive recall have a second check
    (names, the margin to the best match), so a single cut isn't expected to be perfect."""
    p = embeddings.PROFILE
    for name, scale, _, side, pairs in calibrate.CHECKS:
        if name in ("duplicate", "forgotten", "name_match"):
            wrong = [(a, b) for ok, a, b in pairs
                     if (calibrate.similarity(a, b, side, scale) >= getattr(p, name)) != ok]
            assert not wrong, f"{name}: {wrong}"


def test_best_cut_is_the_middle_of_the_gap():
    assert calibrate.best_cut([0.9, 0.95], [0.5, 0.7]) == pytest.approx(0.8)


def test_reembed_fills_in_missing_vectors_and_recall_finds_them_again(store, driver):
    from companion.reembed import reembed

    store.apply(Extraction(memories=[MemoryOut(text="Pytest's son Logan has a fever", kind="event", importance=6)]))
    store._q("MATCH (m:Memory {user: $user}) REMOVE m.embedding")  # as if made by another model
    assert store.recall("how is Logan feeling?")["semantic"] == []

    counts = reembed(driver, user="pytest")
    assert counts["Memory"] == 1 and counts["User"] == 0  # only what was missing
    assert [m["text"] for m in store.recall("how is Logan feeling?")["semantic"]] == ["Pytest's son Logan has a fever"]


def test_a_tombstone_from_another_model_is_ignored(store):
    store._q("CREATE (:Forgotten {user: $user, episode: 'ep_x'})")  # no vector for this model
    assert store._tombstones("ep_x") == []


def test_a_model_that_separates_well_labels_weak_matches_by_its_own_score(store, monkeypatch):
    """Qwen3-8B sets weak_below: its vector score decides, and no cross-encoder runs."""
    import dataclasses

    from companion import store as store_module

    monkeypatch.setattr(store_module, "PROFILE", dataclasses.replace(store_module.PROFILE, weak_below=0.8))
    monkeypatch.setattr(store_module, "relevance", lambda *a: pytest.fail("the cross-encoder ran"))
    store.apply(Extraction(memories=[MemoryOut(text="Pytest's dog Rex is afraid of thunderstorms", kind="fact", importance=6),
                                     MemoryOut(text="Pytest works as an accountant", kind="fact", importance=6)]))
    r = store.recall("my dog hates storms", touch=False)
    assert r["relevance_by"] == "vector score" and r["relevance_min"] == 0.8
    assert {m["text"]: m["weak"] for m in r["semantic"]} == {
        m["text"]: m["score"] < 0.8 for m in r["semantic"]}
    assert not r["semantic"][0]["weak"] and r["semantic"][-1]["weak"]

## LLM settings (lessons 5 and 7–19)

Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint with tool calling works (OpenAI, DeepInfra, OpenRouter,
Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM...). Set in `.env`:

| Key | |
|---|---|
| `LLM_BASE_URL` | e.g. `https://api.openai.com/v1`, `http://localhost:11434/v1` |
| `LLM_MODEL` | chat model name |
| `LLM_API_KEY` | key (any value for local servers) |
| `LLM_EXTRACTION_MODEL` | optional, model for memory extraction (defaults to `LLM_MODEL`) |
| `LLM_TEMPERATURE` | chat temperature |
| `COMPANION_USER`, `COMPANION_NAME` | default user and companion names |

Embeddings run locally by default (`BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5` via fastembed), no key needed.
Lessons 5–7 and the test suite always use that local model. The companion can use a remote
model instead (Lesson 19 has the full table of what runs where).
Lesson 19 switches the companion to a remote model with three more keys:

| Key | |
|---|---|
| `EMBED_BASE_URL` | an OpenAI-compatible `/embeddings` endpoint; empty = local bge-small |
| `EMBED_MODEL` | e.g. `Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-8B`; needs a measured profile in `companion/embeddings.py` |
| `EMBED_API_KEY` | optional, defaults to `LLM_API_KEY` |

After switching, run `.venv/bin/python -m companion.reembed`. The tests always use the local
model. The reranker that labels unrelated recall matches also runs locally (`RERANK_MODEL`,
default `Xenova/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2`, Lesson 18; not used when the embedding profile sets
`weak_below`, Lesson 19). Local models are downloaded once and loaded once per process.

## Tests and evals

Every lesson has tests in [`tests/`](tests), named after it (`test_05_vectors_and_graphrag.py`).

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest                    # unit + database tests: seconds, free (default)
.venv/bin/python -m pytest -m "not db and not llm"   # unit tests only, no Neo4j needed
.venv/bin/python -m pytest -m llm             # LLM evals: real calls, cost money
EVAL_TRIALS=3 .venv/bin/python -m pytest -m llm tests/test_11_extraction_evals.py   # pass rates
```

A `-m` on the command line *replaces* the default `-m "not llm"` in `pytest.ini`, so spell
out `and not llm` when you add your own filter. Database tests never leave data behind: writes run in rolled-back transactions, and memory
tests use their own `pytest` user. A test for a lesson you haven't done yet is skipped with a
reason. [Lesson 0](lessons/00-setup.md#test-it) explains the three kinds of test, and each
lesson ends with a *Test it* section on what its tests teach.

## Common commands

This gives three things:

- **The tests stay local.** `tests/conftest.py` empties `EMBED_BASE_URL` before `.env` loads.
  The test suite runs offline in seconds, pins bge-small's thresholds, and doesn't touch the
  vectors your chats use. `TEST_REMOTE_EMBEDDINGS=1` opts in to the remote model.
- **Switching back costs nothing.** The old vectors are still there.
- **Lessons 5–7** (`embed.py`, `graphrag.py`, `team_agent.py`) keep `LOCAL_EMBED_MODEL` and
  their own 384-dim index.

### Where each model runs, after this lesson

| What | Model | Runs | Why there |
|---|---|---|---|
| Your chats (CLI and web UI) | Qwen3-Embedding-8B, if `EMBED_BASE_URL` is set | remote API | best separation of related and unrelated memories |
| The same, with `EMBED_BASE_URL` empty | bge-small | fastembed, CPU | no key, offline, the course default |
| The test suite | bge-small | fastembed, CPU | offline, free, seconds; pins thresholds |
| Lessons 5–7 scripts | bge-small | fastembed, CPU | the learning examples need no account |
| "Loosely related" labels | the cross-encoder `ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2` | fastembed, CPU | only for models without a measured `weak_below` (bge-small) |
| Lesson 15 graph embeddings | FastRP | inside Neo4j (GDS) | they come from graph structure, not text |

So fastembed stays. It's the zero-setup path, the tests depend on it, and it's the fallback

290-  is then measured on everything that ever went wrong.

**Remote embeddings are now the recommended setup for the companion**
- `.env.example` has the DeepInfra Qwen settings ready to uncomment, marked as the recommended setup. It also says why: the larger model separates related from unrelated memories much better (AUC 0.994 vs 0.854).

- **Thresholds:** tests read them from the active model's settings instead of typed numbers (`test_18`).

content.text:
Yes, I'd switch. Speed isn't the main reason, though. The real gain is reproducibility.

**What's fragile now.** `requirements.txt` only gives minimum versions (`langgraph>=1.2`, `openai>=3.46`…). Someone setting up next spring gets whatever is newest that day, and LangChain, LangGraph and the OpenAI SDK all break things between major versions. Nothing records which versions the recorded outputs and the 197 passing tests came from.

**What uv gives you:**
- **A lockfile (`uv.lock`).** Every reader installs exactly the versions the course was tested with. Upgrading becomes a deliberate step: `uv lock --upgrade`, run the tests, commit.
- **A pinned Python version.** uv downloads the right Python itself, so there's no "my system Python is 3.9" problem.
- **One setup command and no activation.** `uv sync`, then `uv run pytest` and `uv run python -m companion`. `uv run` also re-syncs the environment if dependencies changed after a `git pull`.
- **Much faster installs.** fastembed pulls in onnxruntime and other large packages.

**The costs, which are small:**
- **One more tool to install.** It's a one-line install, and you already have uv 0.11 on this machine.
- **Editing 58 commands.** The docs have 58 `.venv/bin/python …` commands to change to `uv run python …`. That's mechanical. uv still creates `.venv`, so the old commands would keep working anyway.
- **A pip fallback.** Some readers won't want uv. I'd keep a `requirements.txt` generated from the lockfile (`uv export`), so `python -m venv` + `pip install -r requirements.txt` still installs the same tested versions.

**What I'd do:**
1. Add a `pyproject.toml` with the dependencies and the Python version, and generate `uv.lock` from what's installed now.
2. Regenerate `requirements.txt` from the lock, as the pip fallback.
3. Change the setup in Lesson 0 and the README to `uv sync`, with a short pip note, and change every command to `uv run …`.
4. Add a short "Concepts and design choices" row in Lesson 0: why a lockfile, and what pinning costs (you have to upgrade on purpose).
5. Run the test suite through `uv run`, check the links, then commit only when you say.

Should I go ahead with that plan, or switch only the setup lines and leave the existing `.venv/bin/python` commands in the docs as they are?
